sections.heading: DDTC FAQ — ITAR / USML Updates: Australia/UK Exemption & Related Updates
sections.text:
ITAR / USML Updates — Australia/UK Exemption & Related Updates

[KB0012038] Q: How often will the Authorized User list of Australian and United Kingdom parties be updated?

A: The Authorized User list in DECCS is the official, up-to-date record of Australian and United Kingdom Authorized Users. DDTC will update the Authorized User list as needed.

[KB0012020] Q: Can the § 126.7 exemption be used for transfers involving classified defense articles and defense services?

A: Yes. However, consistent with the note to paragraph (b) in § 126.7, compliance with all separate security controls governing the handling of classified articles and services is still separately required.

[KB0012054] Q: If a U.S. company has United Kingdom and/or Australia subsidiaries on its DDTC registration, will these subsidiaries be treated as the U.S. Company?

A: No. Legal entities incorporated in Australia or the United Kingdom are foreign persons, considered to be entities of those countries, and must enroll as Authorized Users through their governments to participate in transfers or activities pursuant to the ITAR § 126.7 exemption.

[KB0012066] Q: Does the expedited licensing procedure outlined in ITAR § 126.15 apply to reexports, retransfers, and temporary imports?

A: No. The expedited licensing procedures apply only to exports of defense articles and services from the United States.

[KB0012024] Q: How do I use the ITAR § 126.7 exemption in the Automated Export System (AES)?

A: Exporters of defense articles must electronically file Electronic Export Information (EEI) using the AES citing code “126.7” in the appropriate field in the EEI for each shipment. This new code appears in the existing AES drop-down menu.

[KB0012028] Q: How do I know if an Australian or United Kingdom party is an "Authorized User" under the ITAR § 126.7 exemption?

A: The list of Authorized Users of Australia and the United Kingdom is available in the Defense Export Control and Compliance System (DECCS). To access the list, you must enroll in DECCS, log-in, and navigate to the Authorized User list.

[KB0012067] Q: The end-users on my license application are all Australian, U.K, or Canadian entities but some intermediate consignees are located in different countries. Is my application still eligible for the expedited procedures outlined in ITAR § 126.15?

A: No. The expedited procedures described in ITAR § 126.15 are available only when the export application would authorize the export of defense articles or defense services to only Australia, the United Kingdom, or Canada. Any application that would authorize exports to parties in any other country will be subject to routine DDTC adjudication processes.

[KB0012052] Q: Will the Authorized User list identify Australian and United Kingdom business registry identification numbers to assist in properly identifying Authorized Users of Australia and the United Kingdom?

A: Not at this time. DDTC is investigating this opportunity in a future update.

[KB0012043] Q: How will Authorized Users who are natural persons be identified on the Authorized User list?

A: Authorized Users of Australia and the United Kingdom who are natural persons will be identified by first name and last name. Verifying such a person’s status as an Authorized User can be accomplished by confirming their first and last name appear on the authorized user list and requesting the Authorized User provide their respective government’s notification of approval as an Authorized User.

[KB0012104] Q: Do Australian and UK parties who would normally be identified as sublicensees on a license or agreement, e.g. subcontractors and suppliers, have to be Authorized Users to receive transfers from other Authorized Users via the § 126.7 exemption?

A: Yes. § 126.7(b)(2)(iii) requires Australian or UK parties be Authorized Users to be an eligible transferor or recipient via the exemption. Whether the party is a prime or subcontractor plays no role in the requirement to be an Authorized User.

[KB0012056] Q: Will a single registration for entities with multiple locations within a country be permissible?

A: Specific in-country locations are not relevant to a party’s Authorized User status. Authorized Users enjoy that status at the name and country level. Authorized User’s headquarters street address is identified on the Authorized User list simply to assist parties in proper identification.

[KB0012042] Q: Can natural persons become Authorized Users?

A: Yes. Any “Person,” as defined in ITAR § 120.61, may become an Authorized User.

[KB0012058] Q: Will additional approvals be required for dual and third country nationals?

A: ITAR § 126.18 may be used in conjunction with ITAR § 126.7, as appropriate, to authorize transfers to dual or third country nationals. ITAR § 126.7 does not itself authorize transfers to dual nationals.

[KB0012018] Q: If I export a defense article to the United Kingdom under the § 126.7 exemption, can the recipient then reexport the item to a party in Australia or retransfer to another party inside the United Kingdom?

A: The ITAR § 126.7 exemption serves as an authorization for the reexport or retransfer of a qualifying defense article to another Authorized User within Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. A defense article qualifies for the § 126.7 exemption if it is not excluded by the Excluded Technology List or “ETL” in Supplement 2 to ITAR Part 126.

[KB0012037] Q: How should I search for Authorized Users in DECCS?

A: Authorized Users who are Australian and United Kingdom parties will be listed alphabetically by legal name. Users may search for the Authorized User ID number, legal name, city, country, and status in a search bar. Users will be able to filter by country and status only.

[KB0012036] Q: Is access to defense articles exported pursuant to the ITAR § 126.7 exemption limited to persons of Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States? May some dual or third country nationals have access, by virtue of having an Australian or United Kingdom security clearance and a need to know?

A: The ITAR § 126.7 exemption only covers transfers within its scope. Other authorities, such as § 126.18, may be applicable to a dual or third-country national who is a regular employee of the recipient Authorized User in-country.

[KB0012048] Q: Will DDTC provide information regarding registration status to Australian or UK Authorized Users in the event a DDTC U.S. registrant has not voluntarily opted in to enable DDTC to share such information?

A: No, DDTC will not provide registration status information with Australian or UK Authorized Users unless a DDTC U.S. registrant has voluntarily opted in to enable DDTC to do so.

[KB0012065] Q: How should I note for DDTC in my license application the fact that the expedited licensing procedures provided for in ITAR § 126.15 apply?

A: DDTC will apply the expedited licensing procedures to export license applications that qualify for expedited treatment under ITAR § 126.15 automatically. There is no need to request expedited treatment specifically. However, applicants always are encouraged to submit any information that they believe would help facilitate an expeditious and streamlined review by the Department.

[KB0012047] Q: How may DDTC U.S. registrants provide their current registration status or, alternatively, voluntarily opt in to have DDTC share their current registration status with Australian or UK Authorized Users?

A: The preferred and fastest method for DDTC U.S. registrants to provide their current registration status to Australian or UK Authorized Users is to furnish a redacted copy of their most recent DDTC registration acknowledgement letter directly to Australian or UK Authorized Users. Alternatively, DDTC U.S. registrants may voluntarily opt in to allow DDTC to share their current registration status (consisting only of their legal name and current registration expiration date) upon receiving an email request from an Australian or UK Authorized User. For instructions on opting in to enable DDTC to share registration status information with Australian or UK Authorized Users, please see the Opt In and Opt Out Guide for U.S. Registrants.

[KB0013178] Q: Are there any territorial restrictions on the § 126.7(c) exemption, similar to those in the § 126.7(a) exemption?

A: Section 126.7(d) does not apply territorial restrictions to the § 126.7(c) exemption. However, the territorial restrictions in § 126.1 do apply to § 126.7(c).

[KB0012060] Q: Does industry have to provide notice of the transfer and wait for approval?

A: No. Authorized Users self-certify to use of the exemption and must comply with all its terms.

[KB0012128] Q: If a U.S. company has legal entities structured as U.S. subsidiaries and U.S. controlled affiliates on its Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) registration, will these subsidiaries and controlled affiliates be considered U.S. Authorized Users?

A: Yes. If a U.S. company has legal entities structured as U.S. subsidiaries and/or U.S. controlled affiliates incorporated in the United States and they are listed in block 8 of its DDTC Registration (form DS-2032), they are considered U.S. Authorized Users.

[KB0012019] Q: If ABC Company United Kingdom is an Authorized User in the United Kingdom, can it transfer U.S.-origin defense articles to XYZ Company Australia in Australia under the § 126.7 exemption?

A: Yes, if XYZ Company Australia is also an Authorized User, the defense article is not identified on the Excluded Technology List in Supplement No. 2 to ITAR Part 126, all other conditions in § 126.7(b) are met.

[KB0012055] Q: Can DDTC confirm that Australian and United Kingdom Authorized Users' subsidiaries or operating divisions in Australia and the United Kingdom will likewise be considered as Authorized Users?

A: This depends on the corporate structure of the Australia or United Kingdom company and its subsidiary or operating division. A subsidiary is its own legal entity and, therefore, must be approved as an Authorized User independently from its parent company to participate in transfers pursuant to the ITAR § 126.7 exemption. An operating division or business unit, on the other hand, is not its own legal entity so would not need to be independently approved as an Authorized User.

[KB0012064] Q: How do I determine whether a defense article or defense service is excluded by the Excluded Technology List (ETL)?

A: The same three-step process may be used for defense services as for defense articles.
First, identify all USML paragraph(s) that describe the article or service. Articles may be described in multiple USML entries.
Second, identify every ETL entry wherein the first (USML Entry) column contains one of the USML paragraphs identified in step one, paying close attention to ranges of paragraphs (e.g., (d) is included in the range “(a) through (e)”) and subparagraphs (i.e., when a category or paragraph is listed in the first column, all of its subparagraphs are as well).
Third, review the text in the second (Exclusion) column of each ETL entry identified in step two, until you find an entry wherein the exclusion text describes the item.
After identifying one entry that excludes the item, you may stop, as the item is not eligible for transfer under the ITAR § 126.7 exemption. If no entry excludes the item, then it is not excluded by the ETL.

[KB0012039] Q: How will the Authorized User list be updated for name changes and mergers and acquisitions? Will there be a gap in Authorized User status to implement those changes?

A: Authorized Users of Australia and the United Kingdom will need to notify their respective government, who will then notify DDTC. There may be a gap in Authorized User status depending on the nature of the name change and the need to update the name on the Authorized User list. The Authorized User list on DECCS is the official list, so parties should ensure the name of the entity they are transferring to via the ITAR § 126.7 exemption is identified appropriately.

[KB0012030] Q: How do Australian and United Kingdom parties become Authorized Users?

A: Australian and United Kingdom parties can apply to become Authorized Users through their respective governments. Australian and United Kingdom parties are required to include a signed and dated Authorized User Terms and Conditions acknowledgment document in their request to enroll. The signer’s name and position must be printed or otherwise clearly identifiable.

[KB0012025] Q: What about Foreign Military Sales (FMS)? Will defense articles exported via FMS be eligible for license-free transfers to Authorized Users pursuant to the ITAR § 126.7 exemption?

A: No. Articles transferred via FMS are transferred based on separate statutory authority and continue to require Third Party Transfer (TPT) approval from the Department of State’s Office of Regional Security and Arms Transfers (RSAT). The ITAR § 126.7 exemption only applies to direct commercial sales (DCS) activities controlled under AECA section 38 and the ITAR.

[KB0012106] Q: Can the § 126.7 exemptions be used for transfers of defense articles, including technical data, originally exported pursuant to an agreement?

A: On September 1, 2024, ITAR § 124.8(a)(5) was amended to modify a clause required in Manufacturing License Agreements (MLAs) and Technical Assistance Agreements (TAAs). Going forward, when this required clause is included in an MLA or TAA, it will enable U.S. and foreign parties to conduct transfers of technical data and defense services that were originally exported pursuant to an MLA or TAA, as well as defense articles produced or manufactured from such technical data or defense services, pursuant to the § 126.7 exemptions.
If your active agreement does not include the updated § 124.8(a)(5) clause referencing § 126.7 but you wish to reexport or retransfer pursuant to § 126.7, the U.S. agreement holder must first amend the agreement to update the subject clause. This may be done as a minor or major amendment. If the agreement is no longer active, e.g., expired or terminated, then an amendment is not required."

[KB0012049] Q: Once a DDTC U.S. registrant voluntarily opts in to have DDTC share its registration status with Australian or UK Authorized Users, does the opted in status ever expire or does it ever need to be renewed?

A: No, once a registrant opts in to have DDTC share its registration status with Australian or UK Authorized Users, the opted in status does not expire and does not need be renewed, unless DDTC registrant opts out.

[KB0012023] Q: Is the ITAR § 126.7 exemption eligible for transfer to an Authorized User on sovereign territories like outlying islands, crown dependencies, forward operating bases in a third country, or vessels at sea?

A: Per ITAR § 126.7(b)(1), the activity must be to or within the physical territory of Australia, the United Kingdom, or the United States.

[KB0012044] Q: Does the ITAR § 126.7 exemption obviate the need to obtain a Foreign Person Employee DSP-5 license for U.S. person employers?

A: The foreign person, in their capacity as a natural person, must become an Authorized User to avail themselves of the exemption. A DDTC authorization (e.g., DSP-5 FPE license) would be required for the transfer of any technical data beyond the scope and limitations of the ITAR § 126.7 exemption. This would include, for example, transfers of defense articles described on the ETL.

[KB0012045] Q: Does the ITAR § 126.7 exemption obviate the need to obtain a U.S. Persons Abroad (USPAB) Authorization?

A: USPAB approvals authorize the provision of limited defense services. The mere presence or involvement of a USPAB during the design, development, etc. of a foreign-origin defense article does not subject the resultant foreign-origin defense article to the ITAR or its reexport/retransfer requirements. In contrast, Authorized Users of Australia and the United Kingdom acknowledge during enrollment that any defense article produced or manufactured with U.S.-origin technical data or defense services transferred via the ITAR § 126.7 exemption will be subject to the ITAR’s jurisdiction. Transferors and recipients should note these important, differing implications in determining which ITAR authorization may be best suited for their needs.

[KB0012053] Q: Will there be a cost associated with Authorized User registration or a required annual fee?

A: There is no cost to becoming an Authorized User or enrolling in DECCS.

[KB0012032] Q: Does my Authorized User approved status expire or is revalidation required?

A: No.

[KB0012029] Q: Who can become an Authorized User?

A: Only parties of Australia, the United Kingdom, or the United States are eligible to be Authorized Users.

[KB0012068] Q: ITAR § 126.15 is available whenever an export "cannot be undertaken under an exemption provided in this subchapter." Is this limited to the AUKUS exemption or will DDTC consider the availability of other exemptions?

A: The expedited procedures are available only when a transfer could not be undertaken pursuant to any exemption provided for in the ITAR. The availability of other exemptions (e.g., ITAR §§ 126.4 or 126.6) will impact whether the expedited procedures in ITAR § 126.15 are applicable.

[KB0012027] Q: Who is eligible to participate in a transfer or activity pursuant to the ITAR § 126.7 exemption?

A: ITAR § 126.7(b)(2) identifies who can participate in a transfer or activity. ITAR § 126.7(b)(2)(i) states U.S. person DDTC registrants who are not debarred under ITAR § 127.7 are eligible. ITAR § 126.7(b)(2)(ii) states U.S. government departments and agencies are eligible. Per ITAR § 126.7(b)(2)(iii), Authorized Users of Australia and the United Kingdom that are identified through DECCS on DDTC’s website are eligible.

[KB0012041] Q: Will the Authorized User list be integrated into common automated screening tools used widely throughout industry?

A: DDTC does not develop or support such third-party screening software and cannot speak to its integration with the Authorized User list.

[KB0012021] Q: Must I obtain a DSP-83 for the transfer of Significant Military Equipment (SME) or Classified defense articles?

A: No. § 123.10(a) excepts the § 126.7 exemption from the DSP-83 requirement. Authorized Users of Australia and the United Kingdom provide nontransfer and use certification through the Authorized User enrollment process.

[KB0012062] Q: Where is the Excluded Technology List (ETL)?

A: The ETL that is applicable to ITAR § 126.7 is codified in Supplement No. 2 to Part 126 of the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR).

[KB0012070] Q: Australia's Department of Defence and the UK's Ministry of Defence are identified as Authorized Users in DECCS. Does this include their service branches, for example, the Royal Australian Navy and the UK's Royal Air Force?

A: Yes. Service branches are Authorized Users by way of Australia’s Department of Defence and the UK’s Ministry of Defence being identified as Authorized Users in DECCS.

[KB0012063] Q: If an item is described on the Excluded Technology List (ETL), is there any carveout that would allow it to be eligible under the ITAR § 126.7 exemption?

A: No. If an item is described on the ETL, it is ineligible for transfer under the ITAR § 126.7 exemption.

[KB0012017] Q: How is the § 126.7 exemption different from the treaty exemptions in § 126.16 and § 126.17?

A: The § 126.7 exemption is authorized under Section 38 of the Arms Export Control Act (AECA), while the §§ 126.16-17 exemptions are authorized by specific treaties. While these exemptions have some similarities (e.g., excluded technologies and pre-vetted parties), the § 126.7 exemption has far fewer requirements and limitations. For example, Authorized Users in Australia and the United Kingdom are approved at the entity level under the § 126.7 exemption, not at the individual facility location level. Additionally, the § 126.7 exemption does not limit end-use and has no unique marking or classification requirements.

[KB0012059] Q: What procedural recourse will be available should any United Kingdom or Australian applicant be rejected?

A: Australian and United Kingdom parties should contact their respective governments for such matters.

[KB0012034] Q: If I am in the Approved Communities under the Defense Trade Cooperation Treaties, am I also considered an Authorized User eligible to use the ITAR § 126.7 exemption?

A: No. Approved Community members who wish to become Authorized Users should contact their respective government to avail themselves of an expedited enrollment process.

[KB0012031] Q: If I am an Australian or United Kingdom party, how do I know if my application to become an Authorized User is approved?

A: Your respective national-level government body will notify you upon a final determination.

[KB0012022] Q: Does the § 126.7 exemption waive the ITAR?

A: No. The exemption allows the transfer of most defense articles and defense services, within defined parameters, without the need to obtain a license or other authorization from DDTC prior to the transfer. Transfers under this exemption remain subject to all ITAR requirements.

[KB0012057] Q: Can one party request the addition of another entity on the Authorized User list?

A: Australian and United Kingdom parties should engage with their respective governments on how to properly submit their request to enroll as an Authorized User.

[KB0012051] Q: Is an Authorized User's contract employee covered by the ITAR § 126.7 exemption?

A: If a U.S. Person contract employee meets the definition of regular employee in ITAR § 120.64, that person is treated like any other regular employee of the Authorized User. If the contract employee is a foreign person, that natural person must become an Authorized User prior to the transfer of technical data, under the authorities of ITAR § 126.7, from the employer to the contract employee.

[KB0012026] Q: Can I use the ITAR § 126.7 exemption if the transfer requires Congressional Notification (CN)?

A: No. The conditions in ITAR § 126.7(b)(4) expressly exclude transfers that trigger a congressional certification (also known as a congressional notification (CN)) under ITAR § 123.15 or § 124.11. Note parties should base their calculations against the ITAR § 123.15 value notification threshold on a per shipment basis.

[KB0012069] Q: Can ITAR § 126.18(e) authorize an Australian or United Kingdom person who is a dual national of a § 126.1 country?

A: Yes. ITAR § 126.1 excepts ITAR § 126.18(e) from its limitations.

[KB0012046] Q: How may Australian or UK Authorized Users obtain the current status of DDTC U.S. registrants?

A: The preferred and fastest method for Australian or UK Authorized Users to obtain the current status of DDTC U.S. registrants is to request a redacted copy of the most recent DDTC registration acknowledgement letter directly from DDTC U.S. registrants. Alternatively, Australian or UK Authorized Users may submit an email request to DDTC to obtain the current status of DDTC U.S. registrants that have voluntarily opted into sharing their current registration status with Australian or UK Authorized Users. For instructions on submitting these email requests to DDTC, please see the U.S. Registration Status Request Guide for Authorized Users of AUS-UK.

[KB0012061] Q: How will the Australian, United Kingdom, and U.S. governments assess an entity in reviewing its request to enroll as an Authorized User?

A: The three governments will leverage existing vetting processes to assess prospective Authorized Users.

[KB0012035] Q: Can parties in countries other than Australia, the United Kingdom, or the United States be Authorized Users or otherwise be eligible to be a party to a transfer under the ITAR § 126.7 exemption?

A: No.

[KB0012050] Q: May DDTC U.S. registrants subsequently opt out of DDTC sharing their current registration status with Australian or UK Authorized Users?

A: Yes, DDTC U.S. registrants that have opted into enabling DDTC to share their current registration status with Australian or UK Authorized Users may subsequently opt out. For instructions on opting out, please see the Opt In and Opt Out Guide for U.S. Registrants. In the event DDTC U.S. registrants never opt into having DDTC share their current registration status with Australian or UK Authorized Users, they do not need to request to opt out.

[KB0012040] Q: How will DDTC and industry track updates to the Authorized User List in DECCS?

A: Parties should reference the Authorized User list prior to each transfer to ensure the recipient is identified as an Authorized User. The Authorized User list will also identify parties whose Authorized User status is suspended or revoked. DDTC does not notify Authorized Users of updates. In instances of suspension or revocation, the entity’s respective government will notify the entity.

[KB0012033] Q: Can my Authorized User status be suspended or revoked?

A: Yes, in instances of non-compliance, failure to respond to DDTC inquiries, or based on other national security concerns.

[KB0012074] Q: How do I access the Authorized Users list?

A: 1. Navigate to deccs.pmddtc.state.gov/deccs
2. If you are already enrolled in DECCS click "Log In". If not, please enroll for an account. For more information on how to enroll in DECCS you can view our user guide and video here.
3. Once logged into DECCS navigate to the "Applications" tab and select AUKUS "Authorized Users"
Note: If you are unable to see the application in your application drop down list, try clearing the history and cache of your browser. Then re-open a new browser window and try the steps above again.

[KB0012016] Q: How does the § 126.7 exemption work?

A: The International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) § 126.7 exemption simplifies the transfer of ITAR-controlled defense articles, including technical data, the performance of defense services, and engaging in brokering activities between and among Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States within an approved Authorized User group of government, private sector, and research and academic entities. When all requirements are met, parties may engage in such activities without the need for additional Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) authorization. More information on who is an Authorized User is available in a corresponding FAQ.

sections.heading: DDTC FAQ — ITAR / USML Updates: Automated Export System
sections.text:
ITAR / USML Updates — Automated Export System

[KB0011875] Q: When can I use USML Category XXI to export my commodity?

A: Designations of defense articles in USML Category XXI are made by the Director of DDTC’s Office of Defense Trade Controls Policy. USML Category XXI is not a catchall for a wide range of miscellaneous items. Rather, it is a narrowly focused category available when the Director of the Office of Defense Trade Controls Policy determines that an article not enumerated elsewhere on the USML should be included until such time as the appropriate U.S. Munitions List category can be amended.

[KB0010818] Q: If an item is not described in any USML category, may I then self-classify it as USML Category XXI on the license?

A: No. USML Category XXI(a) provides that the Director of the Office of Defense Trade Controls Policy is responsible for making the decision regarding whether an article may be included in Category XXI. If you have reason to believe that an item is not described in USML Categories I-XX and should be included in Category XXI(a), you may request a Commodity Jurisdiction determination.

[KB0011873] Q: Why is a DDTC Determination Number field now required for some Automated Export System (AES) submissions, and what if I don't have a determination number?

A: This field is required only when USML Category XXI is entered in the “DDTC USML Category Code” field. This requirement helps ensure that only commodities that have been determined to be controlled in USML Category XXI by the Director of DDTC’s Office of Defense Trade Controls Policy can be declared as such in AES.
If a user submits a shipment in AES using USML Category XXI without providing a valid determination number, the system will return Informational response code 5C2. See CSMS 54237959 for more information.

[KB0011879] Q: Who do I contact if my AES question is not addressed on the DDTC website?

A: For DDTC Data Elements, please contact the DDTC Response Team at DDTCCustomerService@state.gov | (202) 663-1282. For general AES questions, please contact askaes@census.gov or 1-800-549-0595 Option 1.

[KB0010867] Q: How should items be classified in the Automated Export System for items transitioning to the Commerce Control List but being exported under a legacy State Department authorization?

A: You should enter the USML category as indicated on your license, not the new Export Control Classification Number.

[KB0010868] Q: If I have an EAR-controlled item on a USML license what are the Automated Export System (AES) filing requirements for legacy licenses and new licenses?

A: In both cases, an AES filing is required regardless of the dollar value. For legacy licenses the applicant is not required to file an EAR classification in AES or enter Export Control Classification Numbers (ECCN) on export control documents that accompany the shipment. However for licenses under §120.5(b)(2) received after the effective date of a revised category, the applicant must identify the EAR classification(s) in AES in the ECCN field for all EAR items, as well as provide the EAR classification in accordance with §123.9(b)(2).

[KB0011876] Q: What process should I use to determine the correct USML Category for my commodity?

A: DDTC encourages exporters to self-classify their articles for export when practicable. If you are not the manufacturer of the article, we encourage you to contact the manufacturer or distributor to identify the export jurisdiction and classification of the article you wish to export.
As a starting point, DDTC recommends manufacturers review the Order of Review at ITAR § 120.11 and the USML at ITAR § 121.1. If you have doubt as to whether an article you manufacture is described on the USML, we encourage you to submit a Commodity Jurisdiction (CJ) determination request via the DECCS Industry Portal using form DS-4076 (a process for which DDTC registration is not required). The CJ process is described at ITAR § 120.12. Additional guidance for submitting a CJ request is available on the DDTC website under the Commodity Jurisdictions tab under ‘Conduct Business.’
Exporters may submit an export license application to DDTC in advance of receiving a CJ determination, out of an abundance of caution, using the most reasonable USML entry in Categories I-XX. For more guidance, see the DDTC FAQ, “May I submit a CJ for an item at the same time that I submit a license request to the Department of State for the same item?”
Even if your commodity is not described on the USML, it may be subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) administered by the Department of Commerce. For items subject to the EAR, you may submit a Commodity Classification Request (CCATS) to the Department of Commerce. You may contact the Department of Commerce, BIS Office of Exporter Services for more information at (202) 482-4811.

[KB0011880] Q: Can I use a USML Category XXI determination number that has been assigned to a different commodity?

A: No. Each USML Category XXI determination number applies only to the commodities for which the determination was issued. For example, if a determination number is issued for two specific models of a camera, or for all cameras meeting certain criteria, it cannot be used for cameras that don’t meet those criteria, or for commodities that are not cameras. If you suspect that your commodity should be described in USML Category XXI based on a comparison with similar commodities, you should contact the DDTC Response Team at DDTCCustomerService@state.gov | (202) 663-1282 for assistance.

[KB0011878] Q: Who do I contact if I don't have a DDTC Determination Number for use in the Automated Export System (AES)?

A: DDTC Determination Numbers are issued to manufacturers who have received written confirmation from the Department of State that their items are controlled in USML Category XXI. USML Category XXI is not a catchall for a wide range of miscellaneous items. As a result, it is most likely that your commodity is not controlled in USML Category XXI.
For further information, see “What process should I use to determine the correct USML Category for my commodity?”
Exporters who previously received a USML Category XXI determination from the Department of State but no longer know their determination number can contact the DDTC Response Team at DDTCCustomerService@state.gov | (202) 663-1282 for assistance.

[KB0011877] Q: Who do I contact if the Automated Export System (AES) is not accepting my DDTC Determination Number for USML Category XXI?

A: Exporters who have received a USML Category XXI determination from the Department of State and subsequently encounter difficulty validating that export classification in AES can contact the DDTC Response Team at DDTCCustomerService@state.gov | (202) 663-1282 for assistance.

[KB0010869] Q: For an approved shipment that contains both transitioned and non-transitioned items, what Destination Control Statement (DCS) do I use?

A: Until a "uniform" statement that covers both USML and Commerce Control List items is approved, applicants should include both EAR DCS and the ITAR DCS language for all bills of lading, air waybills, and other shipping documents, and the purchase documentation or invoice. However, to distinguish which phrase applies to which commodity, the EAR DCS verbiage should be prefaced by the phrase, "For items subject to the Export Administration Regulations," while the ITAR verbiage (ref. ITAR §123.9(b)(1)) should be prefaced with, "For items subject to the International Traffic in Arms Regulations."

[KB0010870] Q: What is meant by "commercial invoice" in ITAR 123.9(b)(1)?

A: The term "commercial invoice" references the document that moves with the freight.

[KB0011874] Q: Who has the authority to determine that an item or service is included in USML Category XXI?

A: Consistent with the text of USML Category XXI(a), the Director of the Office of Defense Trade Controls Policy has the authority to decide whether an article may be included in USML Category XXI.

sections.heading: DDTC FAQ — ITAR / USML Updates: Commodity Categorization
sections.text:
ITAR / USML Updates — Commodity Categorization

[KB0010874] Q: The control text for USML paragraph (x) hardware indicates items subject to the EAR may only be included in a license or agreement if USML hardware in the same USML category as the (x) hardware will also be included in the license or agreement. Is this interpretation correct?

A: So long as the items subject to the EAR are to be used in or with the defense articles listed in the same authorization request, and the defense articles are controlled in a category that allows for paragraph (x), then paragraph (x) may be used to export items subject to the EAR for the same USML category. As a general rule, an authorization request where the category of the paragraph (x) hardware does not match the category of the USML-controlled hardware on the same request has a strong presumption of RWA. However, each case will be reviewed separately and adjudicated on its merits before a final determination is made. Note, paragraph (x) may not be used to export items subject to the EAR that are to be used with defense articles not listed on the same authorization request.

[KB0010878] Q: For items that were once subject to the ITAR but that are now no longer within the scope of a USML category, do we need to submit a formal classification request to the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) in order to determine how the item is controlled under the EAR or before submitting a license application to BIS for the item?

A: No. To ensure compliance with the EAR, one must determine whether or where an item subject to the EAR is controlled on the EAR's Commerce Control List (CCL) before exporting or reexporting it. Such determinations are among the first steps in determining whether a license is required from BIS to export or reexport the item. With few exceptions, military items that were formerly subject to the ITAR will be within the scope of one of the CCL's corresponding "600 series" ECCNs. For example, military aircraft parts and components that were once within the scope of USML VIII(h) but that are no longer within the scope of that category or any other USML category are generally now within the scope of ECCN 9A610.x. With few exceptions, satellite-related items no longer subject to the ITAR will be within the scope of the 9x515 or 9x004 ECCNs. One may make classification determinations or decide to submit a license application to BIS without needing to submit a classification request to BIS first. If there is doubt about where or whether the item falls within the scope of one of the EAR's ECCNs, one may seek a formal classification determination (CCATS) from BIS under established procedures.

[KB0010873] Q: A revised category contains the same language as an unrevised category. How will cases for the unrevised category be handled when the revised category goes into effect?

A: The Department reiterates the principle provided in the first rule implementing Export Control Reform: where there is overlap in control regarding a particular article, the control of the revised USML category supersedes that of the unrevised USML category. As such, license not in compliance will be Return Without Action'd.

[KB0010877] Q: I am certain that my product is not subject to the ITAR because it is clearly not within the scope of any USML categories. I am, however, uncertain about which ECCN in the EAR"s CCL would apply to my product. Do I need to submit a CJ request to DDTC to get a determination that the product is not subject to the ITAR before I submit a classification request (a CCATS) to BIS asking for a determination regarding which ECCN applies to my product?

A: No. As described above, one may make jurisdictional and classification self-determinations. If there is doubt about the classification status (i.e., where it is controlled on the CCL) of an item that is clearly not within the scope of the USML, then one does not need to submit a CJ request to DDTC before submitting a classification request (a CCATS) to BIS.

[KB0010872] Q: Do I need to amend my DDTC authorizations if they only contain items moving from on USML category to another?

A: No. Both agreements and licenses are valid until their expiration. However, if a license is to be amended for reasons unrelated to Export Control Reform, then the category designations must be updated as well. For agreements, if a major amendment to an agreement is submitted, category designations must be updated; but if a minor amendment is submitted, category designations do not necessarily need to be updated. Furthermore, during the transition period, when information on an In Furtherance Of license does not match that which was presented in its parent agreement, the applicant should note the disparities on the cover letter (15.1) for that license. For example: "Gas turbine engines formerly designated USML Category VIII(b) here designated as Cat XIX(a)."

[KB0010876] Q: We have been exporting 40mm grenade launchers under Category IV(a) as "–grenades–as well as launchers for such defense articles." With the publication of Rule III, effective July 1, 2014, however, the entry for these articles has been deleted. As such, we are now unsure as to how we should classify the launcher or the 40mm rounds that go with it.

A: Per the "Corrections, Clarifications, and Movement of Definitions" Rule published October 10, 2014, Grenade launchers are captured under Category II(a), "Guns over caliber .50 (12.7 mm), whether towed, airborne, self-propelled, or fixed, including but not limited to, howitzers, mortars, cannons, recoilless rifles, and grenade launchers," while the related grenade rounds are caught under Category III(a), "Ammunition/ordnance for the articles in Categories I and II of this section." Note, rocket-propelled grenades remain under Category IV(a)(12).

[KB0010871] Q: Is it possible for a defense article to be described in multiple entries on the U.S. Munitions List (USML)?

A: Yes, the Order of Review process in ITAR §120.11 allows for more than one category on the USML to apply to a defense article, and as such, you should review all potentially relevant USML entries. As a general rule, in cases where an item is described in multiple entries, an enumerated entry takes precedence over an entry controlling the item by virtue of a specially designed catch-all. The exception to this rule is where a SME entry is involved. In all situations, a SME entry will take precedence over a non-SME entry. Thus, a classified guidance system for a missile should be listed under Category IV(h)(30), which is SME, and not IV(h)(1).
If through the Order of Review, one determines a particular item itself is not specifically enumerated in the USML, it may still be controlled by virtue of its parts and components, which are caught via a catch-all. For example, a part or component of an airborne radar system specially designed for the F-35 may not be enumerated or captured in USML Category XI but controlled under the specially designed catch-all of Category VIII(h)(1).

[KB0010875] Q: If my commodity is not called out specifically in the EAR or the ITAR, do I need to submit a Commodity Jurisdiction Determination Request?

A: If you are unable to determine the classification of an item after reviewing the USML and Commerce Control List per the Order of Review (see ITAR §120.11), you may submit a commodity jurisdiction determination to DDTC.

[KB0010879] Q: DDTC wrote in its April 16, 2013, Federal Register Notice (78 Fed. Reg. 22740, 22750) that "[p]arties making a classification determination or submitting a CCATS are advised that only a CJ determination provides an official and exclusive decision on whether an item is a defense article on the USML." Does this mean that I am not permitted to determine for myself without receiving a CJ determination that a product is or is not subject to the ITAR?

A: No. In order to ensure compliance with the ITAR and the EAR, exporters must make jurisdictional and classification determinations before exporting or reexporting. If there is doubt about whether an item is subject to the ITAR, DDTC has established procedures for processing and issuing a formal determination (CJ determinations) regarding the item's jurisdiction, i.e., whether or not it is within the scope of a USML category. If there is no doubt that an item is not subject to the ITAR, but there is doubt about whether or where the item is within the scope of one of the EAR's ECCNs, BIS has established procedures for processing and issuing formal determinations (CCATS) regarding the item's classification status on the EAR's CCL. The purpose of the referenced sentence is to emphasize that the only official jurisdictional determinations (i.e., whether or not an item is subject to the ITAR) are those issued by DDTC and thus, classification determinations issued by BIS are not jurisdictional determinations. Rather, they are determinations regarding whether or how items not subject to the ITAR are controlled on the EAR's CCL. See 15 C.F.R. § 748.3. DDTC inserted this sentence into the notice because it appeared to DDTC and BIS from their review of the public comments at issue that some were of the erroneous opinion that a classification determination issued by BIS constituted a binding determination by the U.S. Government that the item at issue was not subject to the ITAR.

[KB0010880] Q: I am certain that my product is subject to the ITAR but I am uncertain about which specific USML category paragraph applies to it. Should I submit a commodity jurisdiction request or a general correspondence to get an official resolution of such issues?

A: Commodity Jurisdiction request.

ITAR / USML Updates — Cyprus

[KB0011850] Q: How long will the suspension of the policy of denial for the Republic of Cyprus be in effect?

A: The Republic of Cyprus’ status as a proscribed destination has been suspended for Fiscal Year 2025 (October 1, 2024, through September 30, 2025).

[KB0011851] Q: How does the Secretary's Fiscal Year 2025 certification regarding the Republic of Cyprus (ROC) differ from previous waivers?

A: For Fiscal Years 2021 and 2022, the Secretary of State exercised waiver authorities in the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2020 (P.L. 116-92) and the Eastern Mediterranean Security and Energy Partnership Act of 2019 (P.L. 116-94, Div. J.) to amend the United States’ defense trade policy with respect to the ROC to allow for certain transfers of non-lethal defense articles and defense services after determining such action was essential to the national security interests of the United States.
For Fiscal Years 2023, 2024, and 2025, the Secretary of State certified to Congress that the Government of the ROC is continuing to cooperate with the U.S. government on anti-money laundering regulations and financial regulatory oversight and has made and is continuing to take the steps necessary to deny port access to Russian military vessels for refueling and servicing. The certifications, which must be made annually, allow for the removal of the policy of denial in its entirety for Fiscal Years 2023, 2024, and 2025.

[KB0011852] Q: Does the Fiscal Year 2025 certification impact the Republic of Cyprus' eligibility for the Foreign Military Sales program?

A: No. The certification only impacts the United States’ defense trade policy regarding Direct Commercial Sales.

[KB0011849] Q: What is the current defense trade policy on the Republic of Cyprus and how has it changed?

A: The Republic of Cyprus’ status as a proscribed destination has been suspended for Fiscal Year 2025 (October 1, 2024 – September 30, 2025). This action continues the Department’s current policy, which suspended the status of the Republic of Cyprus as a proscribed destination under § 126.1 of the ITAR on October 1, 2023, for fiscal year 2024.

[KB0011853] Q: Is the Fiscal Year 2025 certification applicable to both the Republic of Cyprus and the area administered by the Turkish Cypriots?

A: The certification is only applicable to the United States’ defense trade relationship with the Republic of Cyprus.

sections.text:
ITAR / USML Updates — Documentation/Recordkeeping

[KB0010887] Q: ITAR § 123.9(b)(2) reads, "When exporting items subject to the EAR on a Department of State license or other approval, the U.S. exporter must provide to the end-user and consignees in the purchase documentation or other support documentation submitted with the Department of State license or other approval request the appropriate EAR classification information for each item exported pursuant to a (USML) "(x)" paragraph. This includes the appropriate ECCN or EAR99 designation." I interpret this to mean that Export Control Classification Numbers (ECCN) must be included on the purchase order supplied as the sole support document to a license application.

A: Not necessarily. The § 123.9 reference to "in the purchase documentation or other support documentation" refers to the end-user and consignees (as in "end-users and consignees identified in") and not to the means by which the U.S. exporter is to convey the requisite information (i.e., ECCNs or EAR99 designation) to the end-user/consignee. While § 123.9 obligates the applicant to provide such information to these parties, it may be conveyed in a manner outside of the license application.

[KB0010886] Q: What happens to record-keeping requirements for items that transition to the Commerce Control List?

A: Records must continue to be maintained for a period of five years following the last transaction, regardless of jurisdiction.

[KB0010882] Q: Do I need to amend my DDTC authorizations if they only contain items moving from on USML category to another?

A: No. Both agreements and licenses are valid until their expiration. However, if a license is to be amended for reasons unrelated to Export Control Reform, then the category designations must be updated as well. For agreements, if a major amendment to an agreement is submitted, category designations must be updated; but if a minor amendment is submitted, category designations do not necessarily need to be updated. Furthermore, during the transition period, when information on an In Furtherance Of license does not match that which was presented in its parent agreement, the applicant should note the disparities on the cover letter (15.1) for that license. For example: "Gas turbine engines formerly designated USML Category VIII(b) here designated as Cat XIX(a)."

[KB0010885] Q: Can I submit a minor amendment to my existing agreement to make use of paragraph (x) or does this require a full amendment?

A: A minor amendment is sufficient for updating an agreement to reflect paragraph (x) components. However, during the transition period, it is not necessary to update an agreement to make use of paragraph (x), provided the paragraph (x) items are already included in section 124.7(a)(1) of the agreement. Authorizations in furtherance of items listed in the agreement may be requested from the Department of State and/or Commerce during this transition phase without amending the parent agreement.

[KB0010884] Q: Does the requirement to supply a purchase order as support documentation for a Technical Assistance Agreements extend to paragraph (x) items?

A: Per § 123.1(b)(1), a purchase order (or the like) must be supplied as support documentation for licenses containing items subject to the ITAR and EAR, whether In Furtherance Of or not. It is not required for the agreement itself.

[KB0010883] Q: Do Technical Assistance Agreement (TAA) Transmittal Letters need to indicate the Export Control Classification Numbers (ECCN) for paragraph (x) items?

A: No, but including ECCNs may speed up processing times.

sections.heading: DDTC FAQ — ITAR / USML Updates: Exemptions
sections.text:
ITAR / USML Updates — Exemptions

[KB0011635] Q: Does ITAR § 126.4 cover exchanges of ITAR technical information during conversations or meetings that may lack written approval from the relevant government agency?

A: Yes. If a transaction involving the transfer of technical data satisfies the provisions of ITAR § 126.4(a) or 126.4(b), then these provisions may serve as the export approval for exchanges of ITAR technical information during conversations or meetings.
Note that under ITAR § 126.4(b)(1), transfers of technical information to a department or agency of the U.S. government are approved pursuant to its “request,” as defined by the department or agency requesting the transfer.
Further, under ITAR § 126.4(b)(2), transfers of technical information to an entity other than the U.S. government or pursuant to an international agreement or arrangement are approved pursuant to a “written request.” For transfers that are oral, visual or electronic the exporter must also complete a written certification as required by ITAR § 120.15(f) and retain it for a period of five years.

[KB0011637] Q: Can ITAR § 126.4 be utilized to conduct classified transfers?

A: Yes, ITAR § 126.4 can be used to conduct classified transfers. Persons who intend to transfer classified defense articles and services, including classified technical data, pursuant to ITAR § 126.4 are required to comply with all certification and filing requirements for significant military equipment and exemptions.

[KB0010888] Q: Part 123.4(a)(5) provides an exemption for the temporary import and subsequent export of unclassified defense articles approved for import under the Foreign Military Sales (FMS) program and executed under a Letter of Offer and Acceptance (LOA). Is there a similar exemption for classified FMS articles?

A: Yes. The import and subsequent export of both classified and unclassified FMS defense items executed under an LOA are examples of "transfers," as described in §126.6(c) of the ITAR. Provided the criteria of §126.6(c) are fully satisfied, you may use the exemption covered in this section.

[KB0010891] Q: Are public universities eligible to use the ITAR 125.4(b)(9) exemption?

A: If a public university is incorporated under applicable U.S. or state laws, such public universities are eligible to use the ITAR 125.4(b)(9) exemption.

[KB0010890] Q: If a U.S. company exports a part to a Canadian company under §126.5, and the part subsequently transitions to the 600 series, can the Canadian company return the part to the U.S. under the authority of the same exemption?

A: Yes, the U.S. party may continue to use the exemption authority under which the part was previously exported for re-import.

[KB0010889] Q: If a U.S. company received a part for repair using an exemption (e.g., 123.4(a)(1)) and that part transitions to the jurisdiction of the Department of Commerce while still under repair in the U.S., can the U.S. company export the repaired part using an exemption or, will the U.S. company need to use the Commerce regulations to export the part?

A: In such instances, the company may use an exemption for the export of the item subject to the EAR, but only if accompanied by a defense article (see § 120.5(b)(2), or the company may use an EAR authorization.

[KB0011634] Q: Can ITAR § 126.4 be used in lieu of obtaining a third party transfer approval from PM/RSAT for articles procured via FMS?

A: No. As stated in ITAR § 126.4(a)(5), “[a]uthorization under this section is for compliance with the ITAR and does not constitute any other U.S. Government approval that may be required prior to the transfer of a defense article, and does not satisfy other obligations of U.S. law or regulation, or applicable government process, procedure, or practice, including the requirement that any export of an item listed on the MTCR Annex receive the case-by-case review called for in the MTCR Guidelines.”

[KB0011630] Q: Does ITAR § 126.4(a)(1)(ii) authorize exports by U.S. contractors supporting U.S. Government programs? Assuming that the parameters of ITAR § 126.4(a)(1)(ii) (A)-(D) are complied with, is this all the authorization a contractor needs to export an ITAR-controlled defense articles for a government program?

A: No. ITAR § 126.4(a) allows transfers by a department or agency of the U.S. government. If a department or agency of the U.S. government is undertaking the transfer, they may do so if the recipient is a U.S. government employee (ITAR § 126.4(a)(1)(i)) or a person or entity in a contractual relationship with the U.S. government that satisfies the conditions outlined in ITAR § 126.4(a)(1)(ii)(A)-(D).
ITAR § 126.4(b) is the exemption available to non-government persons in a contractual relationship with the U.S. Government who wish to export a defense article.

[KB0011638] Q: Can I ask DDTC to issue a determination or an Advisory Opinion that will tell me whether my transaction qualifies for the ITAR § 126.4 exemption

A: No. DDTC does not provide exporters with a determination as to whether or not they qualify for an exemption. DDTC deems that exporters are best positioned to make their own determination with respect to whether their activities comply with available exemptions, including the new exemption contained in ITAR § 126.4(b)(1).

[KB0011632] Q: Can the authorization discussed under § 126.4(b) be verbal?

A: U.S. Government departments and agencies are responsible for developing their own criteria for what constitutes a “request” as discussed under ITAR § 126.4(b)(1) to conduct a transfer on their behalf. The “written direction” required under ITAR § 126.4(b)(2) must be in writing.

[KB0011631] Q: ITAR § 126.4(b) notes that an export can be conducted "on behalf of the U.S. Government" to:
(1) the U.S. Government where requested, or
(2) other entities pursuant to written direction and where an international agreement is in effect.
What separates the exemption under § 126.4(b) from the exemption in § 126.4(a)?
When is one applicable over the other?

A: ITAR § 126.4(b) allows a person or entity other than the U.S. Government to undertake a transfer “on behalf of” a department or agency of the U.S. Government.
ITAR § 126.4(a) allows transfers by a department or agency of the U.S. Government.
The difference between (a) and (b) lies in the person that is undertaking the transfer.

[KB0011636] Q: When utilizing ITAR § 126.4, whose responsibility is it to receive and keep the end-user certification, where applicable? Is this the U.S. Government's, the exporter's, somehow decided between the two, or is this process exempt from that requirement?

A: ITAR § 120.15(e) provides that “[a]ny person engaging in any export … of a defense article or defense service pursuant to an exemption must maintain records of each such export….” This means the person or entity undertaking the transfer is responsible for all applicable filing, record keeping, and certification requirements. The exporter should, at all times, be able to satisfy the relevant record keeping requirements.

[KB0011633] Q: Other than prohibited countries under § 126.1, what's the general breadth of ITAR exports under ITAR § 126.4? Are there portions of the USML where ITAR § 126.4 would be unavailable?

A: ITAR § 126.4 may be used for the transfer of any defense article or the furnishing of any defense service described on the United States Munitions List (“USML”). The plain text of the provision does not limit the scope of the exemption to certain portions of the USML. However, this section does not authorize any transfer that is otherwise prohibited by any other administrative provisions or by any statute or that is inconsistent with U.S. arms embargoes or United Nations Security Council Resolutions (see ITAR § 126.1).

sections.heading: DDTC FAQ — ITAR / USML Updates: Grandfathering/Legacy Issues
sections.text:
ITAR / USML Updates — Grandfathering/Legacy Issues

[KB0010892] Q: How should items be classified in the Automated Export System for items transitioning to the Commerce Control List but being exported under a legacy State Department authorization?

A: You should enter the USML category as indicated on your license, not the new Export Control Classification Number.

[KB0010896] Q: If an exporter has an approved agreement authorizing In Furtherance Of (IFO) licenses for EAR and ITAR commodities, may the exporter choose to later utilize Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) licenses for the EAR commodities instead of utilizing the DDTC IFO licenses?

A: Yes, you may choose to replace your DDTC IFO license with a BIS license for items that have transitioned to the CCL. As a general rule, applications to BIS for such licenses will generally be processed more quickly if you inform BIS that the application is in furtherance of an existing, identified State authorization.

[KB0010895] Q: Do licensing conditions and provisos on existing licenses continue to apply to items that have transitioned to the 600 series?

A: Yes. All items previously exported under a USML authorization continue to be subject to any limitation, proviso, or other requirement imposed by the authorization. Details on how you transition from a State to a Commerce authorization are below:

[KB0010899] Q: In the case of an existing agreement where all hardware proposed for export will be transitioning to the Commerce Control List (CCL), is it DDTC's practice to continue to allow for technical data exports and defense services but not allow for future DSP-5 licenses in furtherance of the agreement?

A: Yes. If defense services will continue to be performed and/or technical data will be transferred even though the hardware has transitioned to the CCL, then the agreement is considered a mixed authorization. The agreement is valid until whichever comes first: (1) expiration, (2) amendment to incorporate Export control Reform-related changes; or (3) two years after effective date of relevant final rule. Beyond two years after the effective date of the relevant final rule, the agreement is no longer valid unless it has been amended. During the transition period, defense services may be provided and technical data may be exported under ITAR §125.4(b)(2), but hardware licenses submitted to DDTC would be Return Without Action'd since they would contain only items subject to the EAR.

[KB0010894] Q: I have a valid ITAR authorization for the export of items transitioning to the Commerce Control List (CCL). Do I need a new authorization?

A: Not immediately. However, the DSP 5 or other authorization may expire more quickly if it has items in it that have transitioned to the CCL. And remember, if you export CCL items under an existing State Department authorization, you continue to be subject to all the provisos and other limitation of the authorization. The below chart outlines how existing authorizations are affected by transitioned items:

May amend (through a DSP-6) after effective date on case-by-case basis.Valid for all items until expiration. May amend (through a DSP-6) after effective date on case-by-case basis.

Agreement may be kept valid beyond the 2 year period by submitting amendment to authorize transitioning items under § 120.5(b)(2).

[KB0010898] Q: We anticipate a number of the articles we manufacture will move to the Commerce Control List (CCL). As a result, our company would potentially need to prepare nearly 400 minor amendments during 2014 and 2015 to identify the transitioning items with their appropriate (x) subcategory, send them out for signature, and eventually conclude them with DDTC. Given there is no inherent change in the scope of these agreements (the same articles are still included; nothing is being added), it seems that a prudent, less burdensome alternative would be to allow these agreements to remain valid until whichever comes first: expiration or full execution of the next major amendment.

A: With regard to agreements, DDTC provided the following transition guidance: "Agreements containing transitioning and non-transitioning items that are issued prior to the effective date of the relevant final rule will remain valid until expired, unless they require an amendment, or for a period of two years from the effective date of the relevant final rule, whichever occurs first, unless otherwise revoked, suspended, or terminated. In order for an agreement to remain valid beyond two years, an amendment must be submitted to authorize the CCL items using the new (x) paragraph from the relevant USML category." DDTC believes the two-year transition period provides a proper balance of adequate time to amend agreements as necessary without prolonging the adjustment time period.

[KB0010893] Q: Can I submit a minor amendment to my existing agreement to make use of paragraph (x) or does this require a full amendment?

A: A minor amendment is sufficient for updating an agreement to reflect paragraph (x) components. However, during the transition period, it is not necessary to update an agreement to make use of paragraph (x), provided the paragraph (x) items are already included in section 124.7(a)(1) of the agreement. Authorizations in furtherance of items listed in the agreement may be requested from the Department of State and/or Commerce during this transition phase without amending the parent agreement.

[KB0010897] Q: The published transition guidance does not address how DDTC will handle export license requests that are still pending once the transition period has passed. Will DDTC issue these licenses or Return Without Action them?

A: DDTC will continue to process and issue licenses for applications submitted prior to the effective date as "pre-Export Control Reform licenses."

sections.heading: DDTC FAQ — ITAR / USML Updates: Hong Kong
sections.text:
ITAR / USML Updates — Hong Kong

[KB0012009] Q: Does this action apply to all end-users in Hong Kong, or just government entities?

A: In accordance with the Executive Order, Hong Kong is now treated as China under section 126.1(d)(1) of the ITAR and there is a presumption of denial for license requests where a Hong Kong person is named as an end-user, licensee (signatory) or sublicensee, or where Hong Kong appears as a marketing, transfer, re-transfer, re-export, sales, or distribution territory.

[KB0012007] Q: The EO provides that the President is terminating export licensing suspensions for exports of defense articles to certain Hong Kong persons. Are exports of defense services to those Hong Kong persons permitted?

A: Section 902(a)(3) of the Foreign Relations Authorization Act, Fiscal Years 1990 and 1991 (Public Law 101-246, 22 U.S.C. 2151 note) prohibits "[t]he issuance of licenses under section 38 of the Arms Export Control Act for the export to the People's Republic of China of any defense article on the United States Munitions List...." As a result, the President is not required to make a determination under section 902(b)(2) of that Act in order for DDTC to authorize exports of defense services to Hong Kong persons. DDTC will review on a case-by-case basis license applications to export defense services to Hong Kong persons who (1) are physically located outside of Hong Kong or the PRC and (2) were authorized to receive defense articles prior to July 14, 2020. Exporters may continue to rely on available exemptions consistent with the provisions of ITAR § 126.1(a).
We refer you to the U.S. Department of Commerce for additional information on exports to Hong Kong controlled under the Commerce Control List.

[KB0012008] Q: I have a previously approved export authorization which names Hong Kong as a transfer territory. Is this authorization still valid?

A: Yes. Current, valid, non-exhausted authorizations naming Hong Kong as a transfer territory are not affected by the Executive Order. At this time the Department is not taking steps to revoke or rescind previously approved authorizations to export defense articles or services to Hong Kong.
