sections.heading: DDTC FAQ — Licensing: Open General License (OGL) Pilot Program
sections.text:
Licensing — Open General License (OGL) Pilot Program

[KB0011831] Q: Can technical data be retransferred or reexported under Open General License (OGL) Nos. 1 and 2 if it was originally exported under a Technical Assistance Agreement (TAA) that remains active? Do foreign licensees need to contact the U.S. applicant to amend the active TAA?

A: Provided the retransfer or reexport satisfies the requirements, limitations, and provisos of the OGLs, technical data can be retransferred or reexported for the purposes described in the OGLs even if it was originally exported under the authority of a TAA that remains active. The TAA would qualify as an approval issued by DDTC pursuant to section 38 of the Arms Export Control Act for purposes of subparagraph (b)(2)(i) of the OGLs, and the OGLs would authorize the subsequent retransfer or reexport without amendment of the TAA.

[KB0011834] Q: Open General License (OGL) Nos. 1 and 2 at subparagraph (b)(2)(vii) limit retransfers or reexports of defense articles that meet or exceed certain specified values. How should persons seeking to conduct activity under the OGLs calculate the value of defense articles to be transferred?

A: OGL Nos. 1 and 2 at subparagraph (b)(2)(vii) refer to the value of a defense article “in terms of its original acquisition cost.” Accordingly, the value of a defense article to be retransferred or reexported under the OGLs should reflect the selling price, or if nominal then the fair market value, of the defense articles without supplementary costs such as packing and freight.

[KB0011822] Q: Can Open General License (OGL) Nos. 1 and 2 be used to transfer defense articles, including technical data, to the United States?

A: No. OGL No. 1 only authorizes retransfers to authorized persons within Australia, Canada, or the UK. OGL No. 2 only authorizes reexports between and among authorized persons within Australia, Canada, and the UK or for-end use by the U.S. Government in those country destinations. Existing exemptions under the ITAR authorize the temporary import of defense articles into the United States under specified circumstances. This includes, for example, the exemptions at ITAR §§ 123.4 and 126.4, among others.

[KB0011882] Q: Can the Open General Licenses (OGLs) be used to reexport or retransfer items subject to the jurisdiction of the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) of the U.S. Department of Commerce?

A: No. Since the OGLs are an “other approval” as defined in ITAR § 120.57(b) and not an exemption, EAR-controlled items need to be specifically identified on the “other approval” pursuant to ITAR § 120.5(b). Neither OGL specifies “commodities, software, and technical data subject to the EAR.” As a result, EAR-controlled items cannot be reexported or retransferred under the OGLs without a separate authorization.

[KB0011817] Q: Why is DDTC implementing the Open General License (OGL) pilot program?

A: DDTC is continuously reviewing options to maintain an effective modern and agile export control system. The OGL pilot program furthers DDTC’s mission of ensuring that our munitions export control system continues to evolve to better advance U.S. national security and foreign policy objectives, in part by facilitating legitimate defense trade with partners and allies, while denying adversaries access to sensitive U.S. technology.

[KB0011821] Q: Can Open General License (OGL) Nos. 1 and 2 be used to export defense articles from the United States?

A: No, OGL Nos. 1 and 2 authorize certain “reexports” and “retransfers” (as defined in ITAR §§ 120.51 and 120.52, respectively) of unclassified defense articles to the end-users and for the end-uses specified in the OGLs.

[KB0011833] Q: How does DDTC define "organizational-level, intermediate-level, or depot-level maintenance" of a defense article for purposes of Open General License Nos. 1 and 2?

A: DDTC relies on the definitions of these terms at ITAR § 120.45.

[KB0011824] Q: Can all legal entities within the same corporate family engage in activity under Open General License (OGL) Nos. 1 and 2 provided that one legal entity in the family is enrolled in an approved community?

A: No. Only the legal entity enrolled in an approved community may receive, retransfer, or reexport defense articles under the OGLs. Other legal entities, including affiliates and parent entities, must enroll separately in the approved community to receive or reexport defense articles under the OGLs.

[KB0011829] Q: Can Open General License (OGL) Nos. 1 and 2 be used to retransfer or reexport defense articles originally exported under a Foreign Military Sales (FMS) case?

A: No. OGL Nos. 1 and 2 at paragraph (b)(2)(i) – (iii) limit their applicability to only defense articles that were originally exported pursuant to a license or other approval issued by DDTC pursuant to section 38 of the Arms Export Control Act (22 U.S.C. 2778).

[KB0011818] Q: Why is DDTC issuing Open General License (OGL) Nos. 1 and 2 as a pilot program? How long will the pilot program be in effect?

A: DDTC is issuing OGL Nos. 1 and 2 as a pilot program pursuant to International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) § 120.22(b), which allows DDTC to provide export authorization for its own initiatives, including pilot programs or specifically anticipated circumstances for which it considers special authorizations appropriate. DDTC considers the activities described in the OGLs to warrant such special authorizations. It is issuing the licenses as part of a pilot program to assess the viability and appropriateness of the open general license concept.
OGL Nos. 1 and 2 will be in effect from August 1, 2022, through July 31, 2026. DDTC will consider reissuing or amending one or both licenses and may extend their duration.

[KB0011832] Q: Can technical data be retransferred or reexported under Open General License (OGL) Nos. 1 and 2 for the purpose of procuring future services for the repair, maintenance, or storage defense articles?

A: No. Technical data may only be retransferred or reexported under OGLs Nos. 1 and 2 for use in the direct provision of services for the maintenance, repair, or storage of a defense article.

[KB0011819] Q: Is DDTC considering issuing additional Open General Licenses (OGLs)?

A: DDTC may issue subsequent OGLs depending on its experience with, and observations made during, the pilot program.

[KB0011830] Q: Does the Canadian exemption at ITAR § 126.5 qualify as "other approval" for purposes of Open General License Nos. 1 and 2 at subparagraph (b)(2)(i)?

A: Yes. ITAR § 120.57(b) defines “other approval” to include “use of an exemption to the license requirements as described” in the ITAR. Accordingly, a defense article that has been properly exported under the exemption at ITAR § 126.5 has been originally exported pursuant to “other approval” issued by DDTC pursuant to section 38 of the Arms Export Control Act.

[KB0011823] Q: My company has one facility enrolled in an approved community. Can my company engage in activities under Open General License (OGL) Nos. 1 and 2 at more than just the one registered facility?

A: Yes. Once a legal entity has one facility enrolled in either the UK or Australian approved community, that legal entity can receive, store, retransfer, or reexport defense articles as permitted pursuant to OGL Nos. 1 and 2 at any location where it maintains operations within the same country (e.g., the UK or Australia, respectively).

[KB0011883] Q: Do the Open General Licenses (OGLs) allow for demilitarization of defense articles?

A: Yes. The OGLs incorporate the definition of “retransfer” at ITAR § 120.52, which includes “a change in end-use or end-user, or a temporary transfer to a third party, of a defense article within the same foreign country.” DDTC considers the demilitarization of a defense article previously exported for a different purpose to constitute a change in end-use requiring authorization from DDTC under ITAR § 123.9. Provided the requirements and limitations of the OGLs are satisfied, the OGLs constitute a DDTC approval for such a change in end-use.

[KB0011827] Q: My UK company is enrolled in the UK Approved Community and employs dual and third country national personnel. Can we retransfer U.S. origin technical data to them under Open General License (OGL) Nos. 1 and 2?

A: The OGLs do not affect or alter any existing ITAR licensing requirements or exemptions with respect to reexports of defense articles to dual or third country national employees. You must have a separate license or other approval to transfer defense articles to dual or third country national employees who are not nationals of Australia, Canada, or the UK. Note that OGL Nos. 1 and 2 also do not permit retransfers or reexports to persons:
“to whom a presumption of denial is applied by DDTC pursuant to ITAR §§ 120.16 or 127.11(a), including, among other reasons, for past convictions of certain U.S. criminal statutes or because they are otherwise ineligible to contract with or receive an export or import license from an agency of the U.S. Government.” Paragraphs (b)(2)(x) of OGL Nos. 1 and 2 .

[KB0011825] Q: Must foreign intermediate consignees, such as freight forwarders, also be enrolled in an approved community or be a Canadian registered person to receive and reexport defense articles under Open General License (OGL) Nos. 1 and 2?

A: Yes. Only the persons identified in paragraphs (a)(1) through (a)(4) are authorized to receive defense articles under OGL No. 1, or to reexport or receive defense articles under OGL No. 2.

[KB0011828] Q: Can Open General License (OGL) Nos. 1 and 2 be used to reexport or retransfer classified defense articles?

A: No. Only unclassified defense articles can be retransferred or reexported under OGL Nos. 1 and 2. Additionally, both OGLs at subparagraphs (b)(2)(iv) and (v) specify additional restrictions on the types of defense articles eligible for retransfer or reexport.

[KB0011820] Q: What types of activity do Open General License (OGLs) Nos. 1 and 2 support?

A: OGL Nos. 1 and 2 are designed primarily to support the mission readiness of Australia, Canada, and the UK by facilitating defense trade activity related to the maintenance, repair, and storage of unclassified defense articles deployed or in-inventory, rather than supporting the acquisition of new equipment or capabilities. An existing exemption in ITAR § 125.4(b)(5) can be leveraged together with the OGLs to authorize transfers of unclassified technical data for operation of defense articles transferred under the OGLs to or on behalf of the authorized government end-users; however, the defense articles must remain within the geographic territories authorized under the OGLs.

[KB0011826] Q: How can I confirm whether an intended recipient of a defense article is a member of an approved community or is a Canadian registered person?

A: Users enrolled in the U.S. Department of State’s Defense Export Control and Compliance System (DECCS) online application can use the Treaty Reference System (TRS) within DECCS to confirm whether a legal entity is a member of an approved community. Approved community members are assigned an Approved Community Identification Number (ACID) once approved for membership in the respective community. The TRS enables searches by the ACID only, therefore users will be required to obtain the ACID from members of the Australia or UK approved communities prior to conducting the search in TRS.
If you still have questions after consulting the TRS in DECCS, please email the DDTC Response Team at DDTCCustomerService@state.gov. Please include the following information in your request:
Name of the legal entity that is the intended recipient;
Whether you are seeking information about the entity’s participation in either the UK or Australia Community;
ACID Number;
Enrolled facility (if known); and
Reported address where defense articles will be received.
A separate online search tool is available to identify persons registered in the Canadian Controlled Goods Program: https://www.tpsgc-pwgsc.gc.ca/pmc-cgp/recherche-search-eng.html

sections.heading: DDTC FAQ — Registration: Brokering
sections.text:
Registration — Brokering

[KB0011072] Q: What is the process for consolidating a manufacturer/exporter and a broker registration?

A: Your active M and K codes will both continue to exist; however, your broker expiration date has been automatically aligned to coincide with your manufacturer/exporter registration expiration date (in DECCS Registration). Registrants will continue to receive two registration complete letters, one for the M code and one for the K code. Each will be placed into the Registrant’s DECCS account. Consolidation of manufacturer/exporter/broker may only occur on a manufacturer/exporter registration. Registrants are not able to add a manufacture/exporter registration type to their existing broker registration.

[KB0011080] Q: What does "owned" or "controlled" by a U.S. person mean?

A: In accordance with ITAR Section 129.2(a)(3) and Note to paragraph (a)(3), "owned by a U.S. person" means more than 50% of the outstanding voting securities are owned by a U.S. person, and controlled by a U.S. person means one or more U.S. persons have the authority or ability to establish or direct the general policies or day-to-day operations of the firm. U.S. person control is generally presumed to exist where U.S. persons own 25% or more of the outstanding voting securities unless one foreign person controls an equal or larger percentage. However, control can be established below the 25% threshold if a U.S. person holds a position (e.g., president/owner/director/senior officer, etc.) where that U.S. person has the authority or ability to establish or direct the general policies or day-to-day operations of the firm, regardless of percentage of voting securities.

[KB0011071] Q: If I am a registered broker may I apply for export licenses under my broker registration (K code)?

A: Brokers may not obtain export licenses. U.S. Brokers that need to obtain export licenses must submit an exporter registration and request export licenses using their exporter registration code.

[KB0011075] Q: Do foreign persons outside the United States that are not owned or controlled by U.S. persons continue to require registration as a broker under ITAR Part 129?

A: Effective October 25, 2013, a foreign person, as defined in ITAR Part 120.63, outside the United States that is not owned or controlled by a U.S. person will no longer need to be registered under ITAR Part 129, unless they perform ITAR regulated brokering activity while in the U.S. or U.S. protected territories.

[KB0011074] Q: What are the Broker Report procedures?

A: Broker reports are due with broker renewal submissions (i.e., for persons already registered as brokers). The report must cover all brokering activity not the subject of a prior broker report. Broker reports must cover all brokering activity up to three months prior to the expiration of your broker registration. For example, if your registration expires at the end of November 30, 2013, then your broker report would cover the period from January 1st � August 31st. For subsequent years, your broker report would include a trailing 12 month period, e.g., September 1, 2013 � August 31, 2014.

[KB0011078] Q: What is the scope of affiliate-to-affiliate provisions?

A: Per ITAR §120.66, an affiliate of a registrant is a person that directly or indirectly through one or more intermediaries, controls or is controlled by, or is under common control with, such registrant. Activity between and among registrant and its affiliates regarding their own defense articles and services is not considered brokering activity as the activity is being done within the family umbrella of owned or otherwise controlled entities and not on behalf of another unaffiliated third party. Affiliate may also be an entity that a U.S. person controls the day to day activities/policies of, even if the U.S. person does not own any portion of the foreign company and/or there is no parent/subsidiary legal relationship between the two parties. The affiliate-to-affiliate provision does not include affiliates performing a brokering activity on behalf of an unaffiliated third party.

[KB0011082] Q: If a consultant, who is registered as a broker, hires another consultant (independent contractor), do both entities need to be separately registered?

A: The consultant's business, which is registered as a broker subject to U.S. jurisdiction, who subsequently hires an independent contractor, would be able to have the contractor covered under the consultant's broker registration to the extent the contractor meets the regular employee definition under ITAR Section 120.64. This would mean that the contractor is in a long-term contractual relationship (one year or more), the contractor works at the U.S. company's facility and under the direction and control of the consultant, works full-time exclusively for the consultant, and executes a non-disclosure certification, etc. If the contractor does not meet the regular employee definition, is subject to U.S. jurisdiction, and will be performing brokering activity, then the contractor would need to have its own separate broker registration. If the contractor is not subject to U.S. jurisdiction per ITAR Section 129.2(a), the contractor would not have to register as a broker under the ITAR.

[KB0011077] Q: Does "any person" engaged in brokering activities, as stated in ITAR Section 129.3(a) mean all persons, foreign and U.S. require registration?

A: In order to determine whether the brokering provisions enumerated in ITAR Part 129 apply, you have to read the regulation in sequence. ITAR Section 129.3 only applies to those persons subject to U.S. jurisdiction, as identified under ITAR Section 129.2(a), who are conducting brokering activities as defined under ITAR Section 129.2(b), who are not specifically exempted.

[KB0011081] Q: If I am a lawyer or consultant providing legal and compliance advice on export transactions is that activity considered brokering?

A: Activities conducted by an attorney, consultant, or any other professional that do not extend beyond the provision of legal or consulting advice to clients on ITAR compliance is not within the definition of brokering activities. For example, advising on the legality of a transaction, such as advising whether a transaction is ITAR compliant, tax rates or other laws may be preferential, drafting of contract terms where parties to the transaction have already been identified by the client, representing your client to a client-identified foreign party, conducting ITAR audits, and/or providing training or assistance with ITAR compliance procedures, are outside the scope of brokering activities. However, this does not mean that there are no circumstances where an attorney, consultant, or any other professional would be a broker. If these persons engage in activities that go beyond providing consulting or legal advice, including being a third party to the transaction, or are engaged in soliciting, locating a buyer or seller, introducing or recommending specific parties, structuring the transaction, marketing, promoting, and/or negotiating ITAR-controlled defense articles and services on behalf of their clients beyond contract terms of already identified foreign parties by your client, then such activities may constitute brokering activities under ITAR Part 129.2(b).

[KB0011084] Q: What are the changes to ITAR Section 122.4 Notification of changes in information furnished by registrants?

A: Effective October 25, 2013, the Department revised ITAR Section 122.4(a) and 129.8(d) to add provisions instructing registrants to notify the Department of the following material changes as part of the registration renewal process: 1) consolidation of a broker registration with a manufacturer/exporter registration; 2) removal of entities not owned or otherwise controlled from registration; and 3) deletions or additions of U.S. Munitions List categories. However, if notification of change is the subject of an internal reorganization, merger, acquisition, or divestiture registrants must notify the Department of all changes in information within five days after the event, including where applicable, the three changes specified above.

[KB0011083] Q: Can exemption in 129.5(b) be used for foreign defense articles/services that fall into ITAR categories referenced in 129.4(a)(2)?

A: No. The exemption in 129.5(b) from the requirement for approval is not available when the subject foreign defense articles/services fall into the ITAR categories referenced in 129.4(a)(2).

[KB0011086] Q: Are pre-contract activities undertaken in support of potential foreign assistance or sales program conducted by a company that owns the defense article considered brokering activity?

A: No. The company is taking action on its own behalf. Ultimately the potential foreign assistance or sales program would potentially result in a secondary sales contract between the USG and one or more companies and when ITAR 129.5(a)(2)(i) and exemption from requirement for approval provisions are met such activity would be exempt from broker approval.

[KB0011085] Q: Where can one read the full text of the changes in the broker regulations?

A: You can read the full text of the changes in the broker regulations in the 78FR52680

sections.heading: DDTC FAQ — Registration: General
sections.text:
Registration — General

[KB0011848] Q: Can I renew and amend my registration at the same time?

A: Yes, but only if an applicant includes administrative, material, and Mergers, Acquisitions and Divestitures (MAD) changes within the annual renewal submission.
However, if the amendment is executed more than 60 days prior to the registration expiration date, then an applicant must submit a standalone amendment via the ‘Amend’ option in DECCS Registration Dashboard.

[KB0012117] Q: What is the Tier 1 discount pilot program and how do I apply/qualify?

A: The Tier 1 discount pilot program allows certain Tier 1 registrants to receive a $500 discount on their registration fee, reducing the total fee to $2,500.
You may qualify if:
$3,000 is equal to 1% or more of your organization’s total revenue for the last calendar year (total revenue means all income your organization received last year, not just sales of ITAR-controlled items), and
You did not receive a favorable determination on a license application or other authorization request during the 12 months ending 90 days before your current registration expires.
How to apply:
Prepare a statement on your company letterhead, dated and signed by a senior officer, confirming that $3,000 is 1% or more of your total revenue for the last calendar year (total revenue means all income your organization received last year, not just sales of ITAR-controlled items).
The statement does not need to be notarized, but it must be accurate and truthful.
Attach this statement as a PDF to block 11 of the DS-2032 form.
Save the document as “Fee Discount Request” and upload it to the Supporting Documentation section when submitting your registration application in DECCS.
Need help?
Email: DDTC Help Desk
Phone: (202) 663-1282 |8:00am – 5:00pm ET

[KB0012114] Q: How were the new fees calculated?

A: The Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) conducted a multi-year assessment to calculate the new registration fees. The new registration fees are based on several factors, including the last 15 years of inflation, technological advancements, and advancements in support services.

[KB0011055] Q: Where do I submit my registration package?

A: Registration submissions must be submitted through DECCS up to a maximum of 60 days but no less than 30 days in advance of the renewal expiration. You may begin updating/editing your Registration up to 90 days prior to the renewal expiration.

[KB0011059] Q: What if the registrant does not receive a notification?

A: If a renewal notification is not received, contact the DDTC Response Team at 202-663-1282 or by email at DDTCResponseTeam@state.gov. The registrant is responsible to ensure fees and renewal submissions are received at least 30 day prior to the registration expiration date. It is recommended that the registrant create a calendar reminder for the upcoming registration expiration date.

[KB0011054] Q: What version of the DS-2032 can be used for electronic submission?

A: The current DS-2032 version posted on the DDTC website must be used for electronic submissions. Older versions of the DS-2032 are not able to be used.

[KB0012116] Q: When are the new fees effective?

A: On December 10, 2024, the Department of State published a final rule (89 FR 99081), regarding the registration fee structure and changes to the three tiers of Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) registration fees. The new rule is in effect as of January 9, 2025.
New Registrants
Effective January 9, 2025, first-time registrants will pay the $3000 Tier 1 fee to register with DDTC. Click here for website guidance on how to create a new registration.
Registration Renewals
For registrations scheduled for renewal, DDTC will continue to send the standard e-mail reminder notifications (90 and 30 days prior to expiration) requesting registrants to log into the Defense Export Control and Compliance System (DECCS) to view the renewal fee and begin the renewal application. Click here for website guidance on how to renew a registration.
Current registrations expiring on or after March 31, 2025, will be issued standard reminder notifications under the new registration fee structure included in the final rule.
Registrants issued 90-day reminder notifications with the registration fee structure under the prior regulation may pay the amount listed in DECCS under DDTC’s prior registration fee structure.

[KB0011053] Q: Is electronic submission of the registration package required?

A: Effective January 1, 2014, registration submissions must be submitted electronically. All physical registration submissions received, post dated after December 31, 2013, will be returned without action with instruction to resubmit electronically. Registration fees will not be returned, unless company is not required to register. Companies must submit their registrations using DECCS.

[KB0012115] Q: When did DDTC announce the new fees?

A: The Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) published a proposed rule on April 2, 2024, proposing changes to the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) registration fee structure and increasing registration fees, and solicited public comments on the proposed changes (89 FR 3119, Apr. 24, 2024) (https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2024-08627).
DDTC carefully considered all comments and published a final rule implementing the changes on December 10, 2024 (89 FR 99081). (https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2024-29032).

[KB0012127] Q: Are there any special circumstances which the Department will consider to delay full payment of the registration fee?

A: Registrants whose fees are greater than $4000 may appeal to the Department for consideration of an alternate payment schedule. To be considered, registrants must provide proof that the registration fee is greater than 1 percent of the total sales in the given year. "Total sales" includes domestic and international sales and is not limited to sales of items controlled on the USML. Applicants must submit a request for special consideration to DDTC not less than 30 days prior to registration expiration. Any request received within the 30-day window will be automatically disapproved.

[KB0012122] Q: What is the registration fee for non-profit organizations?

A: Registrants who are wholly exempt from income taxation pursuant to 26 U.S.C. 501(c)(3) may pay the first tier registration fee of $3,000. Registrants must provide proof of such status (i.e., Internal Revenue Service (IRS) certification form) and submit it with their registration package. The IRS certification must apply to all entities/affiliates listed in the registration submission.

[KB0012113] Q: Are there any other changes to the new fees rule?

A: In the final rule (89 FR 99081), the Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) made the following adjustments to the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR):
A return of the registration fee structure to the text of the ITAR at § 122.3 by making a non-substantive movement of text from ITAR § 122.3 to § 122.2.
Revision of a section heading to better describe content.
Addition of text regarding registration discounts and how to obtain further guidance.
Conforming changes to brokering in ITAR part 129.

[KB0012124] Q: When and why was the registration fee adjusted?

A: On December 10, 2024, the Department published a Federal Register Notice of Final Rule to change the fee structure and increase the registration fees, effective January 9, 2025 - see final rule (see 89 FR 99081).
The registration fees were last adjusted in 2008 (see 73 FR 55439).

[KB0012112] Q: When it comes to registration fee calculations, what is a "favorable determination"?

A: A favorable determination is an approval, an approval with provisos (sometimes also referred to as an approval with conditions), or written authorization from the Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) to conduct an activity regulated by the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR). An application that is returned without action or denied is not a type of favorable determination.

[KB0012126] Q: How will a new registrant know their fee?

A: The fee for first time registrants is set at $3,000 (manufacturers/exporters and brokers). However, persons registering as a manufacturer/exporter may also simultaneously register as a broker with a consolidated DS-2032 Statement of Registration and not be charged a separate broker registration fee.

[KB0011070] Q: What is the President's National Security Directive on Export Control Reform?

A: On January 22, 2008, the President signed Nation Security Presidential Directive (NSPD) 56. The directive mandated a series of reforms in the way defense trade is executed by the executive branch to enhance transparency, timeliness and predictability for industry. These reforms included the process and management improvements, as well as a requirement that DDTC be fully resourced to perform its mission. It also mandated that DDTCs mission be 75 percent self-funded.

[KB0012125] Q: What are the three-tiers for registration fees?

A: (1) Tier 1: The first tier is a set fee of $3,000 per year. This applies to first time registrants. It also applies to those who are renewing their registrations and for whom the Department did not issue a favorable determination on a license application or other request for authorization during the 12-month period ending 90 days prior to the expiration of the current registration.
(2) Tier 2: The second tier is a set fee of $4,000 for registrants renewing their registrations who have submitted license applications or other requests for authorization and received five or fewer favorable determinations during the 12-month period ending 90 days prior to the expiration of their current registration.
(3) Tier 3: The third tier is a calculated fee for registrants who have submitted license applications or other requests for authorization and received more than five favorable determinations during the 12-month period ending 90 days prior to the expiration of their current registration. For these registrants, the fee calculation is $4,000 plus $1,100 times the total number of favorable determinations over five. To ensure fairness to those registrants in this third Tier if the registration fee is greater than 3% of the total value of applications adjudicated, during the 12-month period ending 90 days prior to expiration of the current registration, the fee will be reduced to 3% of such total application value or $4000, whichever is greater.

[KB0012121] Q: How will a registrant that is ready to renew their current registration know their fee?

A: For registrations scheduled for renewal, the Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) will send the standard e-mail reminder notifications (90 and 30 days prior to expiration) requesting registrants to log into the Defense Export Control and Compliance System (DECCS) to view the renewal fee and begin the renewal application. Click here for website guidance on how to renew a registration.
This notification will be delivered to the email address on the current registration unless a material change has been submitted per International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR) 122.4. It is recommended that the registrant create a calendar reminder for the upcoming registration expiration date.

[KB0013134] Q: My Tier 3 registration is up for renewal under the January 9, 2025 registration fee structure. How is my registration fee calculated if some of my licenses received favorable determinations prior to January 9, 2025?

A: Under the January 9, 2025, registration fee structure, the registration fee for renewing registrants is calculated by looking at the quantity of favorable determinations of license applications (or other requests for authorization) during the 12-month period ending 90 days prior to the expiration of a registration (i.e., the look-back period). In the final rule for the new registration fee structure (in effect January 9, 2025), DDTC established the Tier 3 registration fee as a calculated fee for registrants who have submitted license applications or other requests for authorization and received more than five favorable determinations during the 12-month period ending 90 days prior to the expiration of their current registration. For these registrants, the fee calculation is $1,100 times the total number of favorable determinations over 5, in addition to a base fee of $4,000.
For example, if an exporter's registration expired in June 2025, and they had applied for and obtained seven licenses within the look-back period (in this example, from March 2024 to March 2025), the exporter would pay the registration fee prescribed in Tier 3. This would be a baseline of $4,000, plus $2,200 (because there were two favorable determinations obtained above the baseline of five), for a total fee of $6,200.
To learn more about your renewal fee letter, please reference this FAQ: Understanding the Renewal Fee Details Download File

[KB0012000] Q: How can I expedite my registration application to export, reexport, or retransfer ITAR-controlled defense articles to Ukraine as quickly as possible?

A: Requirements to export, reexport, or retransfer defense articles described on the U.S. Munitions List (USML) to Ukraine remain the same as before Russia’s full-scale invasion. This includes the requirement to register with the Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) as an exporter. DDTC is working closely with numerous stakeholders, including international partners, the defense industry, non-governmental organizations, and other U.S. government agencies to expedite the process as appropriate for Ukraine-related exports, reexports, and retransfers.
Registration takes 30 days on average, but DDTC’s Registration, Compliance, and Analysis Division is making every effort to prioritize and expedite registrations related to Ukraine. Applicants should clearly establish that their application is Ukraine-related by submitting a letter attached to the application indicating that the registration is related to Ukraine. Applicants should also include the word “UKRAINE” in the title of this attachment.
Please be advised that while we are working hard to prioritize submissions related to Ukraine, we cannot guarantee any specific processing timeframe. Part of DDTC’s review involves considering whether the applicant has experience in defense trade and can appropriately protect U.S. origin defense articles from unauthorized diversion or misuse. This review can vary in terms of processing time, depending on the circumstances of the case.
If you have additional questions on the registration process, please contact the PM/DDTC Response Team by clicking on the link below, scroll down to the “Response Team” contact information, click on the “Email” button, and send a message to the Response Team that contains as much information as possible about your situation:
https://www.pmddtc.state.gov/ddtc_public?id=ddtc_public_portal_contact_us

[KB0011840] Q: How long does it take to review new and renewal registration submissions?

A: The review process for new and renewal registrations may take up to 30 days. The registrant must register by using DECCS Registration. For renewals, the applicant may begin drafting a renewal registration 90 days in advance of the renewal expiration. The registrant may submit a renewal registration 60 to 30 days in advance of the renewal expiration.

[KB0011061] Q: Can the fee calculation be disputed?

A: If a registrant believes an error has been made in calculating its registration fee, the registrant may submit a written request explaining the basis for the challenge to the calculated registration fee to the attention of the Director of the Office of Defense Trade Controls Compliance. If the registrant's registration is set to expire within 30 days or less, registrants should submit the challenge to the Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) with a completed renewal registration submission.

[KB0011065] Q: How will lapsed fees be calculated?

A: Lapsed registration fees will be calculated using the registration fee structure in place during the period of the registrant's expired registration. See Lapse Fee Guidelines for the Registration Fee Table.

[KB0011064] Q: Will a registrant receive a refund if during the year the part of the company doing ITAR business is sold or closed?

A: Registration fees are not refunded.

[KB0011063] Q: If a registrant has questions on the registration fee, who should they call?

A: The registrant should contact us via the Contact DDTC page.

[KB0011062] Q: Does a registrant's fee calculation change if their registration package is determined to be incomplete and returned?

A: No. A registrant's registration fee calculation does not change if their registration package is determined to be incomplete and returned. However, registrants should make every effort to submit a complete package.

[KB0011066] Q: What types of approved authorizations are used to calculate the registration fee?

A: Authorizations used to calculate the registration fee include DSP-5, -6, -73, -74, -61, -62, -85s, and agreements and their amendments. Cases returned without action and denied cases are not included in the registration fee calculation. Submissions required under 22 CFR parts 123 through 126, which do not require response from the Department (e.g., sales reports), are not counted when determining the registration fee, nor are disclosures or requests for a commodity jurisdiction determination.

[KB0012120] Q: What is the Tier 3 Total License Value (TLV) Discount?

A: Some Tier 3 registrants may be eligible for a discounted registration fee if they have a large number of low value applications. DECCS will determine and apply the discounted registration fee automatically as part of the Renewal Fee calculation using the following 2 step process:
Step 1: Compute the Calculated Fee, Total License Value, and 3% Value amounts.
Calculated Fee = $4,000 + (# of licenses over 5 times $1,100)
Total License Value = Sum of all favorable license values within the twelve-month period
3% Value = Total License Value amount times 0.03
Step 2: Determine and apply the Discounted Fee if appropriate.
If the Calculated Fee amount is less than or equal to the 3% Value amount, then the discounted fee does NOT apply, and the Renewal Fee is the Calculated Fee amount. If the Discounted Fee does apply, then the Renewal Fee is either the 3% Value or $4,000, whichever is greater.

[KB0011330] Q: Can a Manufacturer/Exporter Registration and a Brokering Registration be filed in a single application?

A: Yes, you may file your Manufacturer, Exporter, and Brokering Registration in one Registration application. You will receive a Manufacturer/Exporter Registration complete letter and a Broker Registration Complete Letter available in your DECCS account after payment.

Registration — Joint Venture

[KB0011997] Q: My joint venture (JV) is incorporated in the United States, but management and control are split 50/50 between two foreign persons—can I have my JV register on its own?

A: If an U.S.-incorporated JV is engaged in ITAR activities, but both of its managing members are foreign persons as defined in ITAR 120.63, then the JV must send a registration submission, signed by a U.S. person senior officer, in Defense Export Control and Compliance System (DECCS) Registration to receive its own, separate registration and code. If an U.S.-incorporated JV does not have a U.S. person senior officer, then the JV will either not be able to register with DDTC or it must hire a U.S. person senior officer who has authority to manage the day-to-day operations of the JV. The U.S. person senior officer must sign and submit the DS-2032 form in DECCS Registration to receive a registration and code. Directorate of Defense Trade Controls Office of Defense Trade Controls Compliance (DDTC) registrants participating in a JV engaged in ITAR-related activities with foreign-persons are reminded that foreign-person employees who will receive ITAR-controlled technical data must first obtain appropriate licenses or other approvals.

[KB0011998] Q: How do I register a foreign-incorporated joint venture (JV) in Defense Export Control and Compliance System (DECCS)?

A: If a Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) registrant owns more than 50% of the outstanding voting securities of the foreign JV then the registrant must add the JV to Block 8 of its DS-2032 form as a subsidiary. If a DDTC registrant does not own more than 50% of the outstanding voting securities of the foreign JV, but otherwise manages the day-to-day operations of the foreign-incorporated JV, then such DDTC registrant must add the JV to Block 8 of its DS-2032 form as a controlled affiliate. Otherwise, without U.S. persons managing the day-to-day operations of the foreign-incorporated JV then such JV is not able to be DDTC registered. Alternatively, if the DDTC registrant is a foreign broker and they own more than 50% of the outstanding voting securities of the foreign JV then they must add the foreign JV to Block 8 of its DS-2032 form as a subsidiary and the JV would only be registered as a foreign broker. If the foreign broker manages the day-to-day operations of the foreign JV then they must add the foreign JV to Block 8 of its DS-2032 form as a controlled affiliate and the JV would only be registered as a foreign broker.
DDTC registrants participating in a JV engaged in ITAR-related activities with foreign-persons are reminded that foreign-person employees who will receive ITAR-controlled technical data must first obtain appropriate licenses or other approvals. Special protocols may be appropriate to address the day-to-day involvement of foreign-person personnel including officers and senior managers. Export compliance briefings should be prepared for foreign-person personnel to ensure they understand ITAR-related restrictions as well as protocols/procedures to request access to ITAR-controlled activities (including defense articles, including technical data, and defense services). Furthermore, it is prohibited to perform defense services or export or temporary import ITAR-controlled defense articles to subsidiaries/affiliates located in proscribed countries under ITAR Section 126.1 (for example, the People’s Republic of China, North Korea, Syria, etc.) without first obtaining a license or other approval from DDTC. DDTC registrants should counsel their employees not to discuss the substance of ITAR-controlled technical data with foreign-person employees without a license or other approval. Also, DDTC registrants should ensure all employees are appropriately briefed on their ITAR compliance responsibilities.

[KB0011999] Q: What type of legal entities can be added to Block 8 of a Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) registrant's DS-2032 form?

A: Entities listed as subsidiaries or controlled affiliates in Block 8 of the DS-2032 form must be separate and distinct legal entities from the registrant in the DS-2032 form. Such legal entities will have their own articles of incorporation and/or formation separate and distinct from their parent company.
However, office and factory locations owned by a DDTC registrant, but not separately incorporated from such registrant must not be added to Block 8 of the DS-2032 form as subsidiaries or controlled affiliates. Similarly, a joint venture consisting of certain resources (e.g., joint money, property, effort, and knowledge)
must not be added to the DS-2032 form if such joint venture is not separately incorporated as a distinct legal entity.
If a DDTC registrant operates under a trade name distinct from its legal name, it must not separately list its trade name in Block 8 of the DS-2032 form. Instead, Block 5 of the DS-2032 form affords the registrant the opportunity to distinguish their “doing business as name” from the legal name reflected in their articles of incorporation or formation.

[KB0011996] Q: My Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC) U.S. registered company and another DDTC U.S. registered company each own 50% of an ITAR related legal entity. Which DDTC registrant must add the company to its DS-2032 form?

A: Generally, the DDTC registrant that manages the day-to-day operations of the joint venture (JV), must add the JV to Block 8 of its DS-2032 form as a controlled affiliate. If both DDTC registered parties have equal management control of the JV, the Office of Defense Trade Controls Compliance may consider other factors which may be determinative of control (including but not limited to): responsibilities related to specific ITAR related activities enumerated in the JV agreement, specifically stipulated tie-breakers, arbitration agreements, etc. If the JV has a 50/50 ownership split and is independently managed, then the JV must send a registration submission using a DS-2032 form in Defense Export Control and Compliance System (DECCS) Registration to receive its own, separate registration and code.

[KB0011994] Q: Which Directorate of Defense Trade Controls (DDTC)-registered U.S. joint venture (JV) member holds responsibility for listing the JV on its Statement of Registration (DS-2032 form) in Defense Export Control and Compliance System (DECCS)?

A: The answer will depend on several factors. If a DDTC registrant owns more than 50% of the outstanding voting securities of the JV, then such DDTC registrant must add the JV to Block 8 of its DS-2032 form in DECCS Registration as a subsidiary, so long as the JV is separately incorporated as its own legal entity (i.e., not an unincorporated collection of property and/or assets). Alternatively, if an DDTC registrant does not own more than 50% of the outstanding voting securities of the JV, but otherwise manages the day-to-day operations of the JV, then such DDTC registrant must add the JV to Block 8 of its DS-2032 form in DECCS Registration as a controlled affiliate, so long as the JV is separately incorporated as its own legal entity (i.e., not an unincorporated collection of property and/or assets).
If a DDTC registrant does not own or have ability to manage the day-to-day operations of the JV, the JV must send a registration submission using a DS-2032 form in DECCS Registration to receive its own, separate registration.
To confirm management control by the DDTC registrant, the Office of Defense Trade Controls Compliance may consider (including but not limited to): ownership distribution of the JV, whether the JV has an independent board of directors, terms of the JV agreement, and/or staffing and resources of the JV.

sections.text:
Registration — Mergers, Acquisitions, and Divestitures

[KB0011842] Q: What could cause a delay in the review of my 5-Day Mergers, Acquisitions and Divestitures (MAD) Change?

A: The review time of a 5-Day MAD Change may vary significantly based on several factors, primarily for the following reasons:
A party to the transaction submits a 5-Day MAD Change that DDTC finds to be deficient, requiring the submission to be Returned Without Action (RWA).
A party to the transaction submits a 5-Day MAD Change within a registration renewal that DDTC finds to be deficient, requiring the submission to be RWA’d.
A party submits supporting documents that omit required information, such as ITAR Registration Code, or misidentifies the parties to the transaction.
A party fails to submit a required ITAR 122.4(a) 5-day notice.
A party fails to submit a required ITAR 122.4(b) 60-day pre-notification.
A party’s 5-Day notice does not adequately explain the transaction, fails to identify the surviving and/or expiring ITAR Registration Code, is not on company letterhead signed by a senior official identified in the DS-2032, or lacks other required information.
The size and scope of a transaction (e.g., multiple parties.) may impact review time.
To ensure your 5-Day MAD Change is processed in a timely manner, please review the Sample 5-Day Notice for examples of the required documentation prior to submitting your amendment via DECCS Registration Dashboard.

[KB0011845] Q: What could cause a delay of my ITAR 122.4(b) 60-Day Pre-Notification submission?

A: The review time of an ITAR 122.4(b) 60-Day Pre-Notification submission may vary based on factors that include, but are not limited to:
DDTC receives a 60-Day Pre-Notification that is less than 60-days prior to the transaction’s closing date.
Failure to email the 60-day Pre-Notification submission to PM-DTCC-MAD@state.gov inbox.
Failure to submit ITAR compliance program materials in Microsoft Word format.
Failure to submit a complete 60-day Pre-Notification submission (please see the Sample 60-day Notice for more details).
Failure to respond to requests for additional information which may arise during the 60-day pre-notification review period.
Underlying transaction involves foreign persons (including foreign governments) specified in 22 CFR 126.1.
Transaction entails parallel regulatory obligations (Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS), Department of Justice (DOJ), Federal Trade Commission (FTC) filings, etc.).
A national security risk has been identified.
To ensure your ITAR 122.4(b) submission is processed in a timely manner, please review the Sample 60-Day Notice for examples of the required documentation prior to sending your 60-Day Pre-Notification to PM-DTCC-MAD@state.gov. DDTC may request additional information regarding the submission on a case-by-case basis.

[KB0011667] Q: We have changed our legal business name. Will we keep our registration code? Also, is there anything we need to provide to DTCC?

A: Yes. The registrant will maintain its registration code if it undergoes a legal name change.
In this event, pursuant to Section §122.4(a) of the ITAR, the registrant must submit a notification in DECCS.
Please attach to your notification, the state government legal documentation evidencing the legal business name change or conversion from the old name to the new name (please note that a legal name change is different than an asset sale, which is addressed in a separate FAQ that can be found HERE).
Please click HERE to see the complete list of ‘Mergers, Acquisitions, and Divestitures’ FAQs.

[KB0011846] Q: What documents do I need to submit with my ITAR 122.4(b) 60-Day Pre-Notification submission?

A: An ITAR 122.4(b) 60-Day Pre-Notification submission should include the following items*:
ITAR compliance program materials in Microsoft Word format.
Notification must be submitted on the letterhead of the registered party, signed by a senior officer listed in Block 6 of the DS-2032;
A brief explanation of the transaction (e.g., purchase, merger, etc.);
Anticipated date of the transaction;
DDTC registration codes for all involved parties;
Before and after organizational charts;
Names, addresses, and telephone numbers of all firms involved;
Name of the ultimate as well as intermediate owners;
Indication of whether a CFIUS filing will be submitted;
Statement of Registration Certification (see ITAR §122.2(b)).
* DDTC may request additional information regarding the submission on a case-by-case basis.

[KB0011666] Q: My ITAR-registered company will acquire another ITAR registrant (that is, not an asset sale). Will both registration codes survive post-acquisition?

A: No. Once the required 5-day notifications are submitted, the Office of Defense Trade Controls Compliance (DTCC) will cancel the seller’s registration.
Unless the buyer chooses to dissolve the seller as a legal entity, DTCC will fold the seller under the buyer’s surviving registration as a subsidiary/affiliate.
Please click HERE to see the complete list of ‘Mergers, Acquisitions, and Divestitures’ FAQs.

[KB0011664] Q: My company, which is not an ITAR registrant, just bought an ITAR registrant. Will my company assume the registration code of the ITAR registrant?

A: No. The registration code is an identifier unique to a specific entity. One entity cannot assume another entity’s registration code.
If the parent company wants or needs to register, then the parent company must register in its own name and fold the previous ITAR registrant under the parent company’s registration as a subsidiary/affiliate.
Please click HERE to see the complete list of ‘Mergers, Acquisitions, and Divestitures’ FAQs.

[KB0011844] Q: How long does it take to review an ITAR 122.4(b) 60-Day Pre-Notification submission?

A: ITAR 122.4(b) provides a 60-day review period. This enables DDTC to screen the transaction for any national security concerns and mitigate those concerns where appropriate. For 60-day review purposes, Day 1 is deemed to begin when DDTC determines that the registrant has provided sufficient information in the 60-Day Pre-Notification submission for the review to be conducted. During the 60-day review period, the DDTC Registration Mergers, Acquisitions and Divestitures Team may reach out to the registrant to obtain additional information regarding the transaction. To ensure your ITAR 122.4(b) submission is processed a in timely manner, please review the Sample 60-Day Notice for an example of the required documentation prior to sending your 60-Day Pre-Notification to PM-DTCC-MAD@state.gov.

[KB0011668] Q: My company, which is not an ITAR registrant, purchased the assets of an ITAR-registered company. Will my company assume the ITAR registrant's registration code?

A: No. DTCC would not consider this transaction to be a name change for the purposes of ITAR registration, but rather an asset sale/acquisition.
The registration code is an identifier unique to a specific entity. One entity cannot assume another entity’s registration code. Thus, in this instance, the seller retains its registration code, which it may or may not choose to cancel.
If the buyer will be in the business of manufacturing, exporting, and/or temporarily importing defense articles or furnishing defense services, it must register in its own name.
Please click HERE to see the complete list of ‘Mergers, Acquisitions, and Divestitures’ FAQs.

[KB0011665] Q: My ITAR-registered company has acquired another ITAR-registered company, which will require name, address, and/or registration code changes to existing Department of State authorizations (e.g., licenses/agreements). Will these authorizations transfer automatically once the buyer and seller provide the 5-day notifications to DTCC? Is there anything else I need to do?

A: Submitting the 5-day notifications does NOT automatically transfer Department of State authorizations from one name, address, and/or registration code to another. Pursuant to Section §122.4(a) of the ITAR, both the buyer and seller must provide complete 5-day notifications.
Click HERE.
Click on the Mergers/Acquisitions/Divestitures tab.
Please include the following language (without the quotation marks) in the buyer’s notification:
“(Insert buyer’s name) assumes all rights, responsibilities, liabilities, and obligations regarding the licenses, agreements, or other approvals (including any conditions, limitations, provisos, or amendments), or any requirements under the Arms Export Control Act or the International Traffic in Arms Regulations for the licenses, agreements and other approvals.”
Upon receipt of such a letter, DTCC will issue the buyer an acknowledgment letter.
The buyer should then submit this acknowledgement letter as an attachment to a General Correspondence request (click HERE to access a PDF file with more details).
If the buyer does not take each of the steps described above, a new authorization request must be submitted to DTCL under the buyer’s registration code to engage in activity approved in a prior authorization under the seller’s authorization code.
Please click HERE to see the complete list of ‘Mergers, Acquisitions, and Divestitures’ FAQs.

[KB0011841] Q: How long does it take to process my 5-Day Mergers, Acquisitions and Divestitures (MAD) Change in DECCS Registration?

A: Typically, the review process for a 5-Day MAD Change may take up to 30 days if all parties submit a well-documented and complete amendment. The review time of the amendment may be delayed if the submission is deficient or incomplete. To help ensure your 5-Day MAD Change is processed in a timely manner, verify that you have added or removed any parent entities, subsidiaries, or affiliates from Tab 8 or 9, as applicable to your MAD transaction. Also review the Sample 5-Day Notice for required documentation prior to submitting your amendment via the DECCS Registration Dashboard.

[KB0011843] Q: What documents will I receive from DDTC upon the completed review of my 5-Day Mergers, Acquisitions and Divestitures (MAD) Change?

A: Generic or customized acknowledgement letters and compliance recommendations are provided to the surviving registrant in a transaction, depending on the type of transaction.
If the transaction does not impact existing licenses, the surviving registrant identified in the 5-Day MAD change will receive a Generic Acknowledgement Letter, which acknowledges the MAD change and includes reminders about ITAR compliance obligations.
If the transaction does impact existing licenses, then the surviving registrant identified in the 5-Day MAD Change will receive a MAD Material Change Acknowledgement Letter, which acknowledges that licenses will move from one registration code to another registration code as a result of the MAD change, as well as including ITAR compliance reminders. The MAD Material Change Acknowledgement Letter must be submitted with the registrant’s DS-6004 application to the Office of Defense Trade Controls Licensing (DTCL).
Also, if the 5-Day MAD Change has no relation to a prior 60-day transaction (e.g., United States-to-United States transaction), then the surviving registrant in the 5-Day MAD change will receive General Compliance Recommendations. This is a general set of compliance tips and recommendations not specifically tailored to the registrant.
If the 5-Day MAD change is related to a prior 60-day transaction (e.g., a foreign-to-United States transaction) then the surviving registrant identified in the 5-Day MAD Change will receive Specific Compliance Recommendations, tailored to the registrant based on the compliance program materials the registrant submitted in Microsoft Word format with their initial ITAR 122.4(b) 60-day submission.

[KB0011847] Q: Will I receive an acknowledgment letter once the review of my ITAR 122.4(b) 60-Day Pre-Notification submission has concluded?

A: DDTC will not provide an acknowledgement letter or other certificate of completion upon conclusion of the ITAR 122.4(b) 60-day pre-notification period. The transaction is instead recorded as an update to the registrant’s electronic statement of registration (DS-2032) in DECCS Registration, following receipt of the registrant’s accompanying MAD change amendment, which is required within 5-days of closing pursuant to ITAR 122.4(a). During the ITAR 122.4(b) 60-day pre-notification period, the DDTC Registration Mergers, Acquisitions and Divestitures Team may reach out to the registrant to obtain additional information regarding the transaction.

sections.heading: DDTC FAQ — Violations and Disclosures: General
sections.text:
Violations and Disclosures — General

[KB0011759] Q: I've received a letter, apparently unrelated to any voluntary disclosure I previously filed, with questions from DDTC asking for information. What should I do?

A: If DDTC reached out to you with questions regarding a potential violation that you have not previously reported through a voluntary disclosure, please submit a complete and detailed response, attaching any requested or otherwise relevant documentation following the format and procedures for disclosures outlined in ITAR § 127.12 and reference the DDTC letter and the DTCC case number therein. This is referred to as a “Directed Disclosure.”

[KB0011769] Q: How does DDTC assign voluntary disclosure case numbers? How long from the sender's postmark date does it take DDTC to provide the disclosing party with a voluntary disclosure case number?

A: DDTC’s Office of Defense Trade Controls Compliance (DTCC) assigns a DTCC case number to a new voluntary disclosure or initial voluntary disclosure notification, upon receipt and provides via email the DTCC case number to the disclosing party. Once DTCC receives the voluntary disclosure, a case number is typically assigned within five-to-ten business days.

[KB0011768] Q: How do I submit voluntary disclosure correspondence to the Department of State?

A: DDTC accepts disclosures and related information via email or mail, including overnight delivery. DDTC encourages the disclosing party to utilize the electronic submission option by emailing disclosures and related information to DTCC-CaseStatus@state.gov. If a disclosure cannot be submitted via email, the disclosing party may send a hardcopy to DDTC via mail, including overnight delivery. Please refer to the DDTC website for the physical address to submit your hard copies.

[KB0011766] Q: How can I obtain an extension of time to submit a full voluntary disclosure or other information to DDTC?

A: If you are unable to provide a full voluntary disclosure within sixty (60) calendar days of the initial notification, or by a deadline indicated in other correspondence from DDTC, you may request an extension following the process described in ITAR § 127.12(c)(1)(ii) and (iii). Requests for extensions should be in writing, signed by an empowered official (see ITAR § 120.67) or a senior officer, and submitted in advance of the deadline to allow proper consideration of the request. Such requests must specify what information required by ITAR § 127.12(c)(2) could not be immediately provided, explain the reasons, and identify the date on which you expect to be able to provide the information.
ITAR § 127.12(c)(1)(iv) states that a failure to provide a full disclosure within a reasonable time may result in a decision by DDTC not to consider the notification as a mitigating factor in determining the appropriate disposition of the violation. These procedures should also be followed if you need more time to respond to a DDTC request for information in the context of a voluntary disclosure or other compliance matter, such as directed disclosure. You can submit the request via email to DTCC-CaseStatus@state.gov.

[KB0011770] Q: I submitted a voluntary disclosure. How do I find out the status?

A: If you have an open disclosure with DDTC, please refer your inquiry to the compliance specialist handling your disclosure. If you do not know which compliance specialist was assigned to review your disclosure, please email DTCC-CaseStatus@state.gov.

[KB0011771] Q: Do I need to wait until a voluntary disclosure case is closed before applying for a DDTC license that is related to the matters disclosed?

A: No. After you receive a DTCC case number, you may apply for a DDTC license that is related to the matters disclosed. Please note that your license application must reference the related DTCC case number in the appropriate block of the license application. If you do not yet know the DTCC case number, do not include a placeholder or fictitious number on the license application. Instead, please email DTCC-CaseStatus@state.gov to obtain the actual case number and include it on the application. Submitting an authorization request without indicating that it is related to a violation may constitute an omission of a material fact for purposes of ITAR § 127.2.

[KB0011752] Q: I believe I may have violated the AECA or the ITAR. Am I required to disclose the violation to DDTC?

A: The ITAR mandates disclosures of certain types of violations. In particular, disclosures are required in certain cases involving (1) countries listed in ITAR § 126.1 (see ITAR §§ 126.1(e)(2), 126.16(h)(8), and 126.17(h)(8)), and (2) unreturned temporary exports of personal protective gear (see ITAR § 123.17(j)). Failure to disclose in such cases may itself constitute a violation of the ITAR.
For all other types of suspected violations, DDTC strongly encourages voluntary disclosure pursuant to ITAR § 127.12 by the party that may have committed a violation. DDTC may consider a voluntary disclosure a mitigating factor in determining the administrative penalty, if any, that should be imposed. Failure to disclose a violation may result in circumstances detrimental to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests and will be an adverse factor in determining the appropriate disposition of the violation. DDTC views voluntary disclosures as a positive step toward improving ITAR compliance.

[KB0011804] Q: I am aware of a potential ITAR violation that I did not commit, and the ITAR does not require that I disclose the violation to DDTC. Should I submit a voluntary disclosure?

A: DDTC strongly encourages the submission of tips by any person with information about another party’s potential violation of any export control provision of the AECA, the ITAR, or any order, license, or other authorization issued by the State Department under the AECA.
DDTC encourages a party submitting a tip to provide as much detail about the potential violation as possible. The process, information, and documentation described in ITAR § 127.12 may be helpful in assembling and providing a comprehensive and actionable report. DDTC treats such tips as confidential.
If you would like to report a ITAR violation that you did not commit, you can submit a tip (and request confidentiality, if appropriate) by accessing the DDTC website “Contact Us” page at this link: https://www.pmddtc.state.gov/ddtc_public?id=ddtc_public_portal_contact_us,” then scroll down to “Contact the DDTC Response Team,” and click the “Email” button. The subject line of your email should clearly describe the submission as a notification to DDTC of a potential violation by a third party, rather than a voluntary disclosure. For more information, please refer to the “Report a Violation” page on DDTC’s website.

[KB0011762] Q: How much time do I have to submit a voluntary disclosure?

A: Any person submitting a voluntary disclosure pursuant to ITAR § 127.12 should initially notify DDTC immediately after a violation is discovered and then, if warranted, conduct a thorough review of all defense trade transactions where a violation is suspected (see ITAR § 127.12(c)(2) for requirements). If submitting an initial notification, which does not contain all the information required of a full disclosure, the disclosing party has sixty (60) calendar days from the date of the initial notification to conduct a thorough review of all defense trade-related activities to submit a full disclosure.

[KB0011756] Q: Under what circumstances is it appropriate to submit a voluntary disclosure?

A: Pursuant to ITAR § 127.12, persons who believe they may have violated the ITAR are strongly encouraged to voluntarily disclose the full circumstances to DDTC. ITAR § 127.12 encompasses not only actual violations of the ITAR, but potential violations as well.
For purposes of ITAR § 127.12, potential violations include situations in which you are uncertain whether the events that occurred constitute a violation, as well as situations in which you are uncertain whether events that would constitute a violation have actually taken place. If, after a thorough review, you are unable to determine whether an actual violation occurred, you may provide DDTC, as part of your voluntary disclosure, with a description of your investigation and an explanation as to your inability to confirm the violation.

[KB0011767] Q: What should be included in a voluntary disclosure?

A: A detailed list of the information and documentation to include in a voluntary disclosure submission is provided in ITAR § 127.12(c)-(e). Voluntary disclosure submissions should also include: a first page with the disclosing party’s letterhead; the disclosing party’s contact information (including email address); documentation substantiating any claims made within the submission (e.g., proof of corrective actions, relevant compliance procedures in effect at the time the violation occurred, etc.); and a certification, signed by an empowered official (see ITAR § 120.67) or a senior officer, stating that all of the representations made in connection with the voluntary disclosure submission are true and correct to the best of that person’s knowledge and belief.
Moreover, if the disclosing party wishes to authorize DDTC to communicate directly with a third-party representative, such as a consultant or outside counsel, an empowered official or senior officer of the disclosing party should provide DDTC with a signed note on company letterhead identifying: (1) the name and full contact information of the third-party representative, and (2) the third-party representative’s relationship to the disclosing party. Please note that the third-party representative may not make the certification required by ITAR § 127.12(e) on behalf of the disclosing party.
For more information, please refer to the “Report a Violation” page on DDTC’s website.

[KB0011757] Q: Who can submit voluntary disclosures?

A: Persons who believe they may have violated any export control provision of the AECA, the ITAR, or any order, license, or other authorization issued by the Department of State under the AECA may submit voluntary disclosures pursuant to ITAR § 127.12. Such persons need not be registered with DDTC to submit a voluntary disclosure.
In addition, a third-party representative, such as a consultant or outside counsel, may prepare and submit voluntary disclosures to DDTC on behalf of another (i.e., the “disclosing party”). Although a third-party representative may submit a voluntary disclosure on behalf of the disclosing party, the voluntary disclosure must be on the disclosing party’s company letterhead and, also, include the certification described in ITAR § 127.12(e), which must be signed by an empowered official or senior officer of the disclosing party. Moreover, if the disclosing party wishes to authorize DDTC to communicate directly with a third-party representative, an empowered official or senior officer of the disclosing party should provide a signed note identifying: (1) the name and full contact information of the third-party representative, and (2) the third-party representative’s relationship to the disclosing party.
